speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Having .been called upon yesterday suddenly to consider a motion upon the order paper re telephones in rural post offices, I gave a ruling that, upon more careful and. mature consideration, I am quite sure, would not be held to be well founded. I based my ruling of yesterday upon a motion of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Btain) regarding tire placing of telephones in rural post offices mainly on the general principle that this resolution .appeared to involve a charge upon the revenue and must be considered in 'Committee of the Whole. A careful examination of cases, 'both in England and in this House, shows that where the ex-Mr. BORDEN.
penditure of public money is not directly involved, and the resolution merely expresses .an abstract opinion on a matter which may necessitate a future grant, it may be introduced directly by a private member.
In looking at the authorities I find, in Canadian Commons Journals, 1892, page 133, on a motion moved by Mr. Denison relating to the .deepening of canals, which was of a very similar character and was afterwards withdrawn, no ruling was given. In Canadian Commons Journals, 1897, page 59, .a motion is. presented advocating a bonus on creameries. In that case it was a somewhat similar motion, but would tend more strongly towards a violation of the rule, as it proposed that 'a cent a pound at least should be given upon all butter manufactured in creameries. After that motion had been considered the debate was adjourned and no objection was taken to it. In Canadian Commons Journals, 1899, page 85, we have a motion with reference to indebtedness for seed grain. Mr. Davin, I believe, proposed the motion which, after being debated, was withdrawn and no point of order was raised. These, with a number of other precedents that I have looked up, justify me in. saying that my ruling of yesterday was not exactly sound, but while saying that I would like to quote Bourinot's remarks on the point, because it is a matter that I think the House should take cognizance of in the future. He says:
A practice has grown up in the House allowing the introduction of resolutions by private members, when they do not directly involve the expenditure of public money, but simply express an abstract opinion on a matter vThich may necessitate a future grant.
Then he gives the cases I have quoted here and proceeds:
As this is a question not always understood it may be explained that such resolutions, being framed in general terms, do not bind the House to future legislation on the subject, and are merely intended to point out to the government the importance and necessity of such expenditure.
Referring to this right of members to move such abstract resolutions, all authorities agree that it is one ' which the House exercises, and should always exercise, with very great reserve, and only under peculiar and exceptional circumstances.' Such resolutions are considered virtually ' an evasion of the rules of the House, and are on that account objectionable, and should he discouraged as much as possible.' Nevertheless neither the English nor Canadian House of Commons has ever agreed to the adoption of a rule to fetter their discretion in regard to the entertaining of such propositions.
Therefore, I presume the custom has grown up in that way. It would be in order for the hon. member who had that

motion in charge to move to have it reinstated on the order paper, as otherwise it would be dropped.
I would move that the resolution be restored to the order paper.
Motion agreed to.

I rise to a question of privilege Mr. Speaker. I wish to call your attention and the attention of the House to a dodger which was put in every member's post-office box yesterday under somewhat strange circumstances. It is headed:	The	Canadian government the
tool of combines; $20,000 challenge; By A. E. Watts, of Wattsburgh, B.C. I do. not wish to encourage this dodger to the extent of reading any part of it, further than to say that so far as it is possible and as effectually as it is possible, to call a member of this House, a liar without using that term, he does so. The writer of this is known to me and to several members of this House. He is known to the British Columbia members; he is known to the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) amongst whose constituents he is to be found and I think the hon. member (Mr. Goodeve) will agree with me, that the writer of this dodger is known as what is generally called half-witted. I say this, not for the purpose of speaking lightly of Mr.' A. E. Watts, of Wattsburg, British Columbia, but because it has come to our knowledge officially that during the sittings of the committee, which made an investigation in connection with the lumber combine, the then chairman of that committee, the late Hon. Thos. Greenway had on different occasions to suppress this same Mr. Watts, and on some occasions to do so on my own suggestion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member state his question of privilege and then confine himself as closely as possible to it?

I am getting there, Mr. Speaker, the question of privilege is this: This paper which has been put in every member's box, the postoffice of the House-of Commons has been prostituted in that way, states that I was guilty of a falsehood when I said that the lumber manufacturers* of British Columbia had been guilty of a combine. It also says that I stated what I knew to be an untruth when I said that such a combine, in my belief, existed yet. This has been put in cold print and I therefore am going to do what I am loath to do, pay enough attention to it to prove that my statements were correct in each instance and it will take only a moment to do so. When I spoke on this subject the other day, I read from the official records of the House of Commons Appendix to the Journals, Vol. 42, 1906-07, the report of the committee on this subject, of which I was a member. I shall repeat what I then read:
The British Columbia Lumber and Shingle Manufacturers' Association, and the Mountain Lumber Manufacturers' Association, which, in the opinion of the committee, amount to a combination

They were found, in the opinion of the committee which was made the opinion of the House, to be a combine, which justifies the statement I made that a combine had been proved.
With regard to the other statement, that such a combine existed, I went no further than to say that the reports in the public press made statements and representations that such a combine existed as late as October 9 last, and I read from the ' Winnipeg Telegram ' a despatch of October 10 last, saying that if that report was correct such a combine did exist. I mention these things to put myself right with regard to the dodger which has been anonymously distributed to the members of the House, and I protest, as emphatically as I am able, against our post office being used for such a purpose. In this instance it does not hurt my feelings to be called what is there written about me, but if it is known as a principle that any member of this House who is enough of a cad to. send anonymous communications to every other member with regard to a certain member can do so with impunity, no member will be safe from being embarrassed and harassed by such actions. One can readily understand that if such things are allowed to pass without protest the day will come when a member may say that he has the right to distribute any scurrilous misrepresentation referring to any man's-morals or his family relations and I protest against the post office being so used.
This letter was not addressed, it was distributed and no such use of our post I office should be permitted without the

articles being addressed to the members. I have inquired into the source from which this dodger comes, and I hope the hon. member whom I am about to name wall correct me if I am misinformed, I am informed although I could scarcely credit it, that this sheet of misrepresentations this false dodger, this scandalous article was handed in by the secretary of my hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) with instructions to place one of these slanderous and malicious articles in the box of -every other of the 220 members of this House.

As the hon. member has referred to me, I would ask the privilege Of answering some remarks he has made. With regard to the author of this circular. I need only say he is one of the very prominent lumbermen in British Columbia, a man who has made a very great success of his business and who has large vested interests there.
Is he not generally recognized as half crazy at least?
Not at all.
I rise to a point of order. I believe that on a question of privilege no discussion is allowed.

I was directly appealed to by the hon. member who has arisen to the question of privilege, who certainly was out of order in referring to a past debate and reading extracts already answered, so I am privileged to reply to a question directly asked.
Hear, hear.

I have already stated
that the article is not anonymous, it is openly signed by the author who issued a. certain specific challenge, and he forwarded this to me as the member representing that district, as he had a perfect right to do, and asked that copies be placed in the hands of each member of the House. Under the^ postal Act that is perfectly legal and legitimate. Any member can receive communications from any outsider without payment of postage under the Act, so that complaint also falls to the ground.
In regard to the names the hon. gentleman has undertaken to call myself I have *nothing to say, because from the source from which they come they will have no effect on me. I only make my statement with reference to the gentleman who is one of my constituents and who has openly signed the article which he has written in What he considers to be a fair defence *of an unfair attack made on the lumbering interests of the province of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have only to add regarding this publication to which my at-Mr. KNOWLES.
tention was called, that I made inquiry as to the custom in regard to the use of the post office in such a case. I was informed that such distribution as occurred in this instance is a common practice, that sometimes newspapers or perhaps letters regarding Bills that are coming before the House, or papers of various kinds that are signed, not anonymous, are handed to the postmaster with the request that he place one in each member's box as he would be obliged to do if the communications were addressed to each member, so that the communications may reach the members sooner than they otherwise would. Communications with reference to Bills coming up in committees in a short time are usually distributed in that way and for that purpose. This was done exactly on the same principle and without any knowledge on the part of the postmaster as to the contents of the communication.
I may say as an old member of the House that I know from personal experience that this has been the usual custom and therefore I feel that the postmaster was not blameable in any way for permitting the distribution of this document.

I desire to call the attention of the government to the apparent necessity which exists in some parts of Saskatchewan at least for the supply of seed grain during the present winter for the crop to be sown next spring. I regret that I am not in a position to give any definite information as to how widespread the necessity may be, but from some parts of my district, I have had representations that it may be necessary to distribute seed grain to some men residing on homesteads or unpatented lands.
