As a matter of fact he suffers a depreciation in the price, and the whole country suffers accordingly, while the man who mixed the grain has certainly made a profit. My position is that the interest of the country at large must be protected against the act of the man who is for the moment handling the grain, and who sees perhaps, no moral wrong in it; and there may be no moral wrong, in degrading the grain that has come into his hands.

Although this is a technical question, it is very interesting, and I want to get from my "hon. friend one more idea. Suppose that man buys his grain, not by grade, puts it into his private elevator and mixes it as he pleases, but after that is not given any certificate. Has the country been damaged?

I think the country has been damaged to some extent, but I do not think that it is a case that can be followed up. I do not think that legisla-

tion can be framed to cover such a case, to prevent it and still to keep within the bounds of the rights of property. I think we cannot prevent it although it is a pity that it occurs.

There is one phase of wrong-doing in connection with the selling of wheat that came under my observation last November. I found, when I was in the city of Winnipeg, that a practice had grown up about on the following lines:	We will say that a large commission house was getting in a hundred carloads of wheat a day, shipped by individual farmers, to be sold on their account. This commission house keeps an inspector of its own who goes around with the government inspector and takes a sample from each of these hundred cars. I found that two or three of the large milling concerns keep an inspector at Winnipeg who also goes around with the government inspector and the inspector of the commission house and also takes samples. They would find in the hundred oars a number of cars that graded, say, only number 3 Northern, but as everybody knows a certain number of those number 3 Northern cars would average up well to No. 2 Northern and there would be a difference of two or three cents a bushel between their value and that of the ordinary No. 3 Northern. Here is where the wrongdoing came in. I find that although this commission house sent these cars of No. 3 Northern to their order at Fort William or Port Arthur for storage puposes, the large milling concerns, without the knowledge of the farmers who grew the grain, or the knowledge of the commission house that shipped the grain, and with the connivance and by the authority of the railways diverted the wheat that was shipped to Fort William or Port Arthur to their private mills and there unloaded it. They said:	We will deliver an equal number
of bushels at the same grade. The result was that they would buy an equal number of carloads of the same grade, but a lean No. 3 Northern, a sample that barely squeezed through as No. 3, and they would ship that down to Fort William, without any reference to the farmer who sold the grain or to the commission house which handled it for him. This enabled the milling company to secure a car of grain that was worth from two to five cents a bushel more than the car that was shipped down for storage at Fort William.

That is grand larceny.
it to the minister in order that his department may take cognizance of the fact and see about some way of putting a stop to a practice that looks to me, as my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) says, like grand larceny. These are the facts; at all events they were given to me by the commission house that shipped the grain absolutely as I have explained them. I hope that the department will take some means-I do not know how it can be done-of putting a stop to that practice.
Will the hon. gentleman explain in what way the railway aided that?
It could not be done without the help of the railway.
Just explain it.
I do not know; I was just told that it is done, but I do not know how.
It is a breach of faith on the railway's part against the man who owned the grain.

The commission house said:	It really does not affect us at all,
nor does it affect tire farmer who shipped the wheat to us as we got the price for him at which that grade of wheat was selling on the market. But, the man who loses in the end is the farmer, because that wheat is sent, say, to Fort William or Port Arthur, and the Ontario miller, or the exporter to the old country, buys No. 3 Northern but gets a leaner No. 3 Northern than he would have got if all the wheat that was graded No. 3 Northern had been shipped direct to Fort William and had gone into storage.
And the country's reputation at large suffers.
There would be a higher average grade whi/ch would enable the': farmer in the end to get more for his wheat.
Would the substituted wheat be shipped out in the same car?
No.
Then that would be easily detected because the shipping bill would show the number of the car in which the grain had been originally shipped?
Yes.
The shipper and the transferee, from the shipping bill, would know that it was not the same car.
That is done in hundreds and hundreds of cases and it is going on to-day. I am just mentioning

It is done on the same principle as that which has taken place time and again at Fort William and Port

Arthur. Supposing they had received in the elevators 3,000,000 or 4,000,000 bushels of wheat to be held in storage for farmers waiting for a rise in price; cases have come to our knowledge in which the big elevator men have sold every bushel of such wheat and it has been shipped to the old country while the farmers were still paying storage on it. I only draw this to the attention of the minister in order that he may make some inquiry and ascertain to what extent it is being done. There should be no difficulty in putting an absolute stop to it. When a commission house ships a carload of wheat to Fort William to go into storage that car should go to Fort William and go into storage and no milling company or anybody else should be allowed to divert that wheat to the use of any other persons without the knowledge of the farmer or the commission house and substitute therefor a oar of inferior wheat.
Would the public ownership of elevators affect that situation at all?

Not that I can see. I think this is one of the easiest matters to remedy now that the attention of the department has been called to it. It was not generally known; at least, I had never heard of such a thing being done. I do not think that the ownership of the elevators at Fort William or Port Arthur would affect that particular phase of the evil.

I -would like my hon. Mend (Mr. Turriff) to make his ease a little more definite. It is like hunting for a needle in a hay stack with the information he has given to me. A commission house did a certain thing and gave certain information. What is the commission house and what is the information? If my hon. friend will put me into communication with the commission house and_ let me know the exact transaction I will carry it a little farther.
I will give my hon. friend the names of the commission house and milling company that were mentioned to me.
I would be very glad to have them. Under the best laws you can have, frauds may be committed, but I do not know whether it is I who should look after such *a fraud or the courts of law.

It is a fraud on the part of the railway company; that is quite clear. The railway company has undertaken to deliver certain, identical goods at a certain place and if the railways have this to their discredit also that they cannot be trusted to deliver goods
given to them then it is time we knew it and took steps to put an end to that practice.
The commission man is at fault there.
No, they are both at fault. A railway that allows a thing like that is not to be trusted in any case.
That might be done either by neglect or by malpractice on the part of an under official of the railway.
But they are responsible.

And the railway management might not know anything about it at all. My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) in the conduct of his own business cannot have his eye on every transaction and some of his officials may slip a cog and he is responsible, but he might be in blissful ignorance of it until it was brought to his attention. I remember seeing in the correspondence that a car was sent to 4 wrong destination presumably for the benefit -of the milling company, and on being traced it was found to be due to the neglect or worse of an under -official, but the railway company righted the matter the moment it knew of it. I do not think a railway company could exist long if it were guilty -of practices of that kind.
If it does exist it should be stopped at once.
Certainly-

Nothing will tend so much to lower the reputation of Canadian wheat as practices of this kind. There has been too much interlocking _ of directors between the milling companies and the elevator companies and the railway companies, and that generally results to the detriment of somebody. The railways will have to be put on their honour to stop this practice or else told that they will be up against the law.

The law on the matter is perfectly clear. When the railway company receives grain for carriage and issues the bill of lading it is responsible for the identical goods until these goods are delivered to the consignee or the consignee's assignee at destination. If, in the interim, any person takes away from the company grain which belongs to the owner of the bill of lading he is liable under the Criminal Code for taking that which does not belong to him. The law is perfectly clear.
[DOT]3321

It only requires, as I should judge, to be applied to the particular case mentioned by the hon. member for Assiniboia.

Assuming that everything was as has been stated the commission house lost nothing, the farmer lost nothing. the railway company lost nothing, so that they were not interested in enforcing the law, and the milling company gained and the credit of the country's wheat lost and ultimately the farmers' price would be depressed.
And wrong-doing was encouraged.

It is because of the conditions that surround the carriage of grain in bulk, which conditions lend themselves to things of that kind, that this complicated' machinery becomes necessary, and that we establish a Board of Commissioners. It is unquestionably probably the most important part of the adminis-' tration of the Grain Act to see that the credit of the country's wheat is not degraded. The country's interest in the preservation of the standard of the country's wheat is far more important than the question of the private rights of the different parties.

We have indeed spent a most profitable hour in discussing this question of mixing. I had a fair idea of the question before, but after the discussion it is much clearer to me and I compliment the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) for the plain way hq has etated the case. I *understand his argument to be that the identity of the grain is a public asset, and if the purchaser mixes before the inspection certificate was given and has it sent over without any inspection, he is reaping an advantage at the expense of the country by appropriating; to himself profit at the expense of the identity of that wheat. The law puts in a concrete form that public asset and demands that it should have an inspection certificate. Under that inspection certificate the producer of the grain may own the grain absolutely, but he does not own the asset known as the inspection certificate, it being an asset in which all are interested, and particularly the producer. If a fraud is perpetrated upon that, he who perpetrates the fraud is guilty of appropriating to himself what does not belong to him in any sense and he gains an advantage at the country's expense.
Hear, hear.
That is the kernel of the whole cause of mixing, and if we grasp it we will he able to cure the evil much more quickly.
After a certificate is issued giving the grade of the grain, how will the mixing thereafter be prevented?
The whole machinery of this legislation is for the purpose of preventing such mixing.
But mixing has occurred.
It is said to have occurred contrary to law, and it is with a view still further to prevent its occurring that we are trying to improve the law.
Would government ownership of the elevators prevent that practice to any greater extent than if the elevators were owned by a elevator company or the carrying the company?
I am not so sure on that point. JSo long as the carrying company keeps its hands off the grain trade it seems to me that would fulfil all requirements.

So long as the Canadian Pacific railway owned and operated their terminal elevators at Fort William I never heard of any complaint about mixing in the Canadian Pacific Railway elevators. Their only interest was in carrying the wheat, storing it, and sending it forward. But during the last few years, the difficulty has cropped up in the case of the American grain companies who have leased from the Canadian Northern and others some of these terminal elevators, and also control by subsidiary companies- a line of elevators in the interior out on the prairie.
That is a very different thing from the elevators being owned and -operated by the railway companies, simply as a convenience for the handling of grain and also . to make, perhaps, a small profit, but there was no object in the railway companies degrading a grade or trying to turn out No.
2 Northern, where they took in No. 3. It is the ownership of the terminal elevators by the same interests that own and control the interior elevators that has largely brought about the whole trouble that the farmers have had 'to complain of during the last few years.
There is more than that.
There may be more than that.

I have always held that the only way we can remedy that is by the government operation of terminal elevators. I understand that most of the mixing has been done at the terminal elevators. We have had instances. The same thing occurred at Duluth. One hundred thousand bushels of No. 1 Northern, 100,000 bushels of No. 2, and 100,000 bushels of No. 3 went info the elevator at the ter-

minal. But what did they send out? They sent out about 150,000 bushels of No. 1 Northern. They got that by mixing in these terminal elevators and raising a No. 2 Northern to a No. 1. I stated last year and I repeat that we want the men who operate these terminal elevators to absolutely have no commercial interest in the grain. If I talked an hour I could not make that any plainer.

That covers the whole thing.
On section 58, weight of bushel.

I am not making this as a suggestion, but might there not be an advantage if the weight of our bushel of oats was made the same as the American? At present the American standard bushel is 32 pounds, while ours is 34 pounds.

What
does my hon. friend think about it?
I think it would be, but I have not given the question * enough consideration to express an opinion that would be worth very much.

I am
something like my hon. friend in that, and so 1 : ok the weights as they were generally agreed upon.
The present weight is really below the average.

That is a good thing, to keep the quality well up.
On section 59, fees.

I wish to enter the same objection to this section as to two others that we have discussed. In my judgment these fees are vexatious without being remunerative and should not be imposed. I would again reserve the right of discussing this on the third reading.

I have some very interesting figures on fees, but I shall withhold them until the occasion tc which my hon. friend refers when we might have the whole matter up at once.
On section 62, appointment of weighmas-ters.

I wish to amend this section by adding after the word ' minister ' and before the words ' may appoint,' the words ' on the recommendation of the board.' The amendment explains itself.
Section as amended agreed to.	*

After the word ' cargo ' I propose to add ' but no certificate shall be issued if scales appear to be defective.' As the clause actually reads it would almost mean that every weighmaster, or assistant was in fact bound to give a certificate. I think it is a fair safeguard to Mr. SCHAFFNER.
put at the end of the clause that no certificate shall- be issued if the scales appear to be defective.
What is the necessity of the words 'upon demand'?
It means that every weighmaster or assistant shall give a certificate when asked to do so.

I want to point out to the minister that under the law some of the weighmasters appointed at the terminal elevators throughout the country now, do weigh the grain, but, if the owner does not demand a certificate he is not obliged to pay any fees. The present clause states that the weighmaster shall give a. certificate upon demand. I think if the weighmasters have complete control, and have to give certificates they ought to be obliged to give certificates whether the owner demands them or not. I also think the fees should be paid whether a certificate is demanded or not.
The fees are always paid, or, if they are not, the weighmaster is not getting his dues.

The weighmaster attends to the weighing, but when it comes to collect the fees the owner of the grain simply says he did not demand a certificate, and in that way gets out of paying the fees. That is an abuse which is actually existing at some of the terminal elevators.
There have been cases of that kind, I am informed; but they have been followed up and the weighmasters eventually collected the fees.

I think the idea of this Act is to provide the fees necessary for the carrying out of it. Now, a shipper from the west sends his grain down through these elevators. It comes through the terminal elevator at Port Arthur and is weighed there, but the shipper does not demand any certificate, consequently the weighmaster does not collect any fees. That is something which is actually going on, and, to avoid it in future I think the words ' upon demand ' should be cut out altogether, making the clause read:
Every such weighmaster or assistant shall give to' any person having weighing done by him a certificate under his hand showing the amount of each weighing, the amount No. of each car or cargo weighed, the initial of the car, the place where weighed, the date of weighing and the contents of the car or cargo.
Then, the weighmaster could collect his fees.

Subsection 2 of section 62 provides that the weigh-

masters and assistants shall receive such compensation, by fees or otherwise, as is determined by the Governor in Council, upon recommendation of the board. That fixes the principle that they shall be paid. Once the principle has been established that there are to be weighmasters, and that there are to be fees for the weighing, as I understand it, the object of section 66 is to make it impossible for a weighmaster or assistant to refuse a certificate.
Under the old Act the, shippers evaded paying the fees altogether by simply not demanding a certificate.

I do not see that there would be anything wrong in I'.aving it read in this way:
Every such weighmaster or assistant shall give to any person having weighing done by him a certificate, etc.

Assuming the principle is thus made obligatory do not the words now proposed to be added take away from the obligation, because the weighmaster may say ' these scales appear to be out of order, therefore I will not give you a certificate
Mr, FOSTER (North Toronto). These words are simply for the protection of the man buying or selling.

Instead of giving any one an opportunity for not issuing their certificate, would it not be better to have a certificate obligatory, and, if the scales appear to be out of order have that fact stated on the face of the certificate.
The idea is to get perfect and correct weighing.

I think the Weights and Measures Act provides that all scales must be tested at certain intervals, and if anyone uses a defective scale he is liable to a heavy fine. That comes under the Inland Revenue Department, which assumes responsibility for the correctness of the scale.

I think it might he as well to let the section stand altered as suggested, and I will make a note of it. We can deal with it later on.
Section allowed to stand as amended.
On section 67-record of weight,
Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto) moved the adoption of section 67, as follows:
All weighmasters and their assistants shall make true weights, and keep a correct record of all weighing done by them at the places for which they are appointed, in which record shall be entered an accurate account of all grain weighed, or the weighing of which was supervised by them or their assistants, giving the amount of each weight, the number of 744
each car weighed, the initial letter of each ear or the name of each vessel, the place where weighed, the date of weighing, and the contents of the car or cargo; if the car is leaking or in bad order the record shall state the fact.
2. An extract from the record kept by any weighmaster or assistant in pursuance of this section, certified by the chief inspector or the chief weighmaster of the division, or by any officer iin the office of either of them, shall be prime, facie evidence of the facts set forth in such extract.
Section 67 carried without discussion.
On section 68-fees,
Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto) moved the adoption of section 68 as follows:
The fees for the weighing -of grain shall he such as are determined by the board which, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may increase or reduce them.	-

I would not take the same objection to this section as I have taken to previous sections relating to fees, but I would direct the attention of the hon. minister to subsection 2 of section 62, which provides for the payment of weighmasters in such a way as is determined by the Governor in Council, suggesting the idea that they may be paid by fees.
I would like to say I think it is objectionable that permanent officials holding such responsible positions as those of weighmasters should have to depend upon fees for their remuneration. I do not think they are paid by fees at the present time. I believe they are paid a salary. I think it is not desirable to have a suggestion in the Act that they should be paid otherwise than by fees. If the hon. minister agrees with me, I would like to be strong on that point.

I find that at the present time, so far as the Georgian Bay ports are concerned? they are all paid, by fees. Peterborough is paid by salary. I note the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), and I will look into the matter. As a rule payment by fee is not the best way. I wish to make a little change in this section No. 68. I propose to take out ' which,' making it read * determined by the board, with the approval of the Governor in Council.
Is that necessary? Drop out ' which ' and let the sentence end at * council.'
Yes, that would cover it.

Before we leave section 67, I hope the minister will take a little suggestion from me. There is always a difference between the amount of grain weighed into the vessel at the terminals

at Port Arthur and Fort William, and the amount taken out at the foot'of the lakes. A year ago these differences made a total of 180,000 bushels. Some vessels are a thousand or fifteen hundred or even two thousand bushels short. Now, the vessel men say that that grain cannot take wings as it comes from the lakes, and they account for the difference in this way:	The grain is weighed by the
government weighmaster as it goes into the shipping bin, in which bin there is a spout going into the vessel. They say that the company that owns the elevator shuts off the spout before all the grain is out of the bin, and they come out at the end of the season ten or twenty thousand bushels ahead of the game.
Impossible!

Well, as I have said, the vessels coming down the lake had an aggregate shortage of 180,000 bushels. I would like to see a subsection added to section 67 to the effect that in -weighing grain into the vessel, the weighmaster shall be responsible for seeing to it that the shipping bin is empty before it is closed off. The minister could have a subsection drafted to meet this very troublesome situation which now gives [DOT]rise to differences and lawsuits among shippers, ship owners and the elevator men. The minister will remember that there was a great scandal about it a year or more ago. It was said that the elevators were full of grain that nobody owned.
These difficulties have occurred and do occur. But could not the question be disposed of under section 69 which, provides that the board may make rules and regulations for the weighing of grain.
And the minister will see to it that the board does that?
I will see to that.
All right,

I think this all bears out my suggestion that the weighmasters, above all others connected with the service should be paid a salary and should have no interest whatever in a fee. They should be men of the highest and of most assured reliability; and in order to secure that class of men permanent salaries must be provided.

I suppose that the present system has arisen out of the variations in the work the weighmasters have to do; some weighmasters have a great deal to do, and in such cases a. salary could Be paid, but others have Mr. CURRIE.
very little to do, and it would be difficult to represent by a salary their real earnings.

The records of the elevators year by year would show what passes through the eievator, and would to a certain extent, be a guide as to what each officer should be paid. I quite agree that these officers should be independent. And I really think the minister ought to provide a corps of Northwest Mounted _ Police to see that these things are carried out. If that were done, I do not think we should have all these grain growers coming down here asking the government to take over the terminal elevators.
The shippers want that as well as the grain growers.
Everybody in the business gets robbed.

Mr. Chairman, we have made very good progress, I am sorry that I cannot go on with this Bill to-night, but I hope to take it up to-morrow.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Reress.
House resumed at eight o'clock.
Air. MONK, moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

['And American companies.
Mr. PELLETIER-and American companies. I think it is the bounden duty of this government to do something in this respect. I have been asked, as the head of the Post Office Department, to give my views on this matter to a certain number of important newspapers in London, England. I have put it over my signature that we are not satisfied with the present system, and rates although they have been reduced to a great extent, and that we expect better for this country .in future, and that we must and are bound to get a cheaper means of cable communication. My words may appear strong, blit they are not any stronger than I think they ought to be.
On all these important questions I am happy to see that both sides of the House agree in believing that the government will endeavour to, and will succeed in doing its full duty.
Amendment, Mr. Maclean (South York), agreed to.
Mr. MONK moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.']

I am sorry the Minister of Railways is not in his seat, as I wished to invite his attention to a matter of considerable importance to eastern Canada, I presume that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will bring the matter to the attention of his colleague, the Minister of Railways. Recently, instructions were sent from the Railway Department at Ottawa to Moncton to the effect that no family passes or trip passes for employees were hereafter to be issued without referring the matter to Ottawa. This was at variance with the long established custom that has obtained on the railway. There were certain rules defined by the department whereby the employees could get, for certain members of their families, at stated intervals, trip passes. A protest was sent to the minister, with the result that the instructions were recalled, and it is now left to the departmental officials tat Moncton and along the line to issue these trip passes. Accompanying the instructions relating to passes to employees and their families was an order to the effect that no passes could be issued to newspaper editors or reporters along the line, as had been the custom in
I

the past, without first referring the matter to the minister at Ottawa. The newspaper men naturally complain, and say that this is practicality withdrawing from them the transportation privileges which have been hitherto accorded to them without exception, for many years, aid along the line of the Intercolonial. ' These trip passes are given to reporters at times, on application of the *editorial management, to attend gatherings, inquests, and all occasions when newspaper men are expected to be hi attendance. They also say that under the new order tile occasion when transportation is required has in some instances long passed before they can get any word back from Ottawa. I think their complaint is well-founded. The government railways should be operated on the same principle as a corporation railway, subject to certain well-defined rules, giving the general manager and the officials of his office discretion to administer the rules which have been made by the department at Ottawa. I wished to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to this matter on behalf of the newspapers of the maritime provinces.

I regret that the Minister of Railways is absent at this moment. I suppose my hon. friend had not notified him that he would bring this matter up, otherwise I am sure lie would have been here. I understand my hon. friend's complaint to be that, under the old usage, the families of employees -were entitled to free transportation without interference from the head of the department, and that now the rule is that to secure such transportation there must be a reference to the head of the department.
That has been recalled by the minister within the last few days.

With some modification, I understand. With regard to newspaper representatives, transportation could be obtained without reference to the head of the department. I understand my hon. friend to say that that rule has been changed, and he would like to seq it restored, so that representatives of newspapers may obtain free transportation.
In accordance with the general rules which have been clearly defined.
I will see that the remarks of the hon. gentleman are communicated to the Minister of Railways.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext:
I desire to direct the attention of the House to the need of improving the parcel post
system we now have in this country. This question has been up a great many times in the House, and I believe the late government had a policy for the expansion of our parcel post system in order to give the people a much better system, and what w'ould be practically an improvement of the express system. We have accepted the principle of parcel post service in Canada already. We have had for years a parcel post which gives fairly good service. The trouble with it has been that it was limited in the weight of the parcels carried, and perhaps the tolls charged were not as moderate as they should be. But for years raid years now we have had a parcel post system, and session after session there has been an attempt made in the House to extend that system; it has been discussed also., in connection with the excessive rates now charged by the express companies on parcels. My idea in substance is this, that if we expanded our parcel post system at the persent time, the effect would be that the express rates would be cut in two tomorrow, and the public of Canada would have relief to that extent. The people of the Canadian west, who to-day have enormous railway grievances of one kind and another, at a time when they feel the condition of affairs to be onerous, would have a reduced express service. That service would be cut in two, practically, to-morrow, if we expanded our parcel post system on the very lines that I believe had been arranged by the late government, reference to which was made the other night, and reference to which I intend to make later on.
Now, if any one has any doubt of the efficacy of the parcel post to-day, I would like to hear the argument presented. I think the parcel post has been absolutely successful wherever it has been tried. Every-nation that has adopted it, with the exception of Canada, has expanded it and extended it by increasing the weight of the parcels to be carried, and they have done it with great and lasting service to the public. Great Britain has been one of the most successful countries in administrating a parcel post system, she has led the world in the matter of postal progress. At one time, I believe, a letter cost a shilling in Great Britain, but now, owing to her almost free postal system, the price of letter postage was reduced from time to time, until it has attained its present very low figure. We have had the same experience, so has the United States, namely, that in proportion as you improve the postal system, and as you reduce the cost of postage you increase the service rendered to the public, and in that way, you help along the progress of the country. Now, I wish to find out either from the present Postmaster General or the late Postmaster General what was the proposal that was before the

late government for two or three years, and which, according to a statement made here the other night, was blocked in the last session, and could not therefore be put into effect. As I understand the matter, it requires no further legislation to extend the parcel post system, all it requires is an order in council. There is a provision in the law now to do so, it is all a matter of policy, and to my mind it is largely a matter of the opinion of this House whether we shall have a parcel post system to-morrow, greatly extended, or not. Seven or eight years ago I brought into this House a motion to regulate the charges of express companies in connection with the Eailwa.y Act. Session after sesion I brought motions forward in that direction. But after several defeats, and after a good deal of hard fighting, those of us who favoured the proposal at last induced the government to put the express companies under the regulations of the Railway Act; so that we have already made some progress. But they are not very extensive. The fruit growers have complained time after time about the exorbitant express rates, and, do what we like and argue what we like, there is very little hope of relief from the express companies or the railway corporations until this country goes into active competition with the exprelss companies through the medium of the parcel post. Public competition is the one thing which will bring the express companies to a sense of their duty to the people and compel them to reduce their charges.
I want to refer for a moment to this principle of public competition. I spoke of it in the House the other day and I return to it to-night, It is the only available weapon in the hands of parliament, the legislatures and the municipalities, to bring private corporations exercising public franchises to a sense of their duty and to a realization of the service which they ought to give and especially the rates which they ought to charge. We have in the province of Ontario embarked in what are called municipal enterprises and we have begun in many of our towns and cities to run our own street railway systems and to generate and distribute our own electric power. We have gone a step further and now we have formed a great combination of municipalities to buy electric power at Niagara Falls and distribute it throughout the province of Ontario. The greatest and the most successful experiment in regard to public ownership, the public control and distribution of a great utility, is in the province of Ontario in connection with the Hydro-Electric Commission, the men who administer it and the associated municipalities. The result of public competition Mr. MACLEAN (South Tork).
in Ontario in connection with electrical energy has been that prices have been cut in two and further reductions are promised. If there is one thing that the people of Ontario believe in-and the people of Ontario are as progressive as those of any other section of the country- it is in the efficiency of public competition in connection with a public service, to improve the service and to cut the rates in two, or even to reduce them more than half. Every municipality in Ontario that has tried public competition in this respect, either in connection with the HydroElectric Commission or of its own motion, has succeeded not only in cheapening the price but in doubling and trebling the use of the utility by the people. When you reduce the cost you increase the use of the utility in a greater proportion. So, the people of Ontario know the efficacy of public competition. They know what public competition can do to increase a service and to reduce its cost.
My argument here to-night is that if we were to put our parcel post system in operation on . an extended scale, if we were to increase the weight of parcels and improve the service, and if we made the delivery of parcels a part of the service, it would have the effect of improving the service and reducing the rates of the parcel post, and not only reducing the rates of the parcel post, but compelling express companies to follow in the same way, that is improve their service and reduce their rates. It does not require any more legislation. The legislation is on the statute-book. All it requires is an order in council. If we establish this principle in connection with parcel post, and if we compel the railway companies to reduce their express charges it follows, as night follows day or day follows night, that all we have to do is to intimate to the telegraph companies that unless they cut their rates in two or reduce them greatly the government will be compelled to go into the telegraph business. We have legislation now on the statute-books which will allow us to go into the telegraph business. If we once make the railway companies understand that government competition will come against them if they do not treat the public fairly, reduce their rates and give a better service, they will be very quick to give a better service and to cut their rates. If we wish to help the people of the northwest with regard to the conditions which prevail there, and railway grievances form the great bulk of their troubles, the time is now and the method to adopt at the outset is an extension of the parcel post system.

The people of the United States are today agitated over a parcel post system. They have never had it. As I have said in this House time after time, the reason they have not had a parcel post system in the United States up to date is that- the railway lobby has been so strong that they have been enabled to defeat every proposal for a parcel post system that came up in Congress. But the day of the supremacy of the railways is at an end. A committee in the recent session collected a great deal of information on the matter, a Bill has been introduced, or is now about to be introduced into Congress, and both parties are committed to put it through. In a very few days you will see the Americans with a first-class parcel system. They see now what can be done in this connection. Only a year ago or less they introduced for the first time, the postal savings bank system against the opposition of the National banks, and all the other banking institutions of the United States. But the savings bank in connection with the post office now has got more business than it can do, and yet the proposition was at the outset that the Postmaster General should try only a limited number of offices. But, day by day, he has extended that system of post office savings banks, and to-day one of the things that the American people are most interested in in the way of recent legislation is the measure which inaugurated the post office savings bank, and the result is that they are determined to have a parcel post system. The American post office to-day is carrying parcels for the British parcel post, and delivering them through the United States. It has to do it because of the International Postal Treaty. It is carrying those parcels for people in Great Britain who wish to send them to the United States, and it is delivering them all through the United States for one-quarter what the express companies charge. The people are finding out that they could send a parcel to England, mail it there and have it delivered, but for the duty, at a cheaper rate than the express companies would charge at any point in the United States.
There is a great argument against the expansion of the parcel post system in this country. I have tried to find out what it was, and I have heard it stated in this House at times. When I came to follow it up, the argument, outside of that of the railway companies who wish to maintain the monopoly that they at present have, Is that it would be hard on the country storekeepers. I have heard men say in this House, it has been written in the press, and I have heard on the platform, that if the parcel post system were extended it would hurt the country storekeeper, and
would be for the advantage of the large departmental stores in the cities, and those stores which carry on what is known as a mail order business. That may be; but there never was an improvement introduced that did not hurt somebody. The steam railways put the stage coaches, horses, country inns and blacksmiths along the roads, out of business, and in that way there was a grievance against the railways. But look at the advantage which came to the general public from the improvement in the speed and comfort of travel.
The world will progress and the old order must give place to the new, and even if it be a disadvantage to the country storekeeper, it is the good which it will do to the general community that must prevail. Think of what an immense advantage it would be to the settler away out on the prairie to be in touch not only with the country store, but also with the base of supplies. I know any number, of instances where when a part of an agricultural implement was needed in a hurry and it had to be sent by express, the express charge was greater than the original cost of the article. That should not be. We have one railway 'in Ontario under public ownership, but I am sorry to say that the express charges on that railway are about as high as they are on the corporation roads. It is not right that the settler in that portion of Ontario should be handicapped by these unnecessarily high rates on the government road. If the people in other countries have the advantage of this enlarged parcel post system why cannot the people of Canada have it? So far as I can find out the block has been caused by the express companies who use the country storekeeper as a buffer between them and an extended parcel post; the voice may be the voice of Jacob, but the hand is the hand of Esau. When John Wanamaker was Postmaster General of the United States he announced in public that he would like to give the people the advantage of an enlarged parcel post, but there were four great reasons blocking the way and these were the four express companies which were allied with the railway interests. Amt these reasons exist in Canada to-day, and they will block the proposal as long as the people allow them to do so. We have fourteen thousand postmasters in Canada every one of whom could become a parcel post agent with a trifling addition to his salary, while to-day the railway and express companies have only their agents at the different railway stations. See what an advantage it would be if every postmaster could handle parcels. And then, consider what a centre of life it would be if we had in every village a post office where parcels could be handled, a telephone office and perhaps telegraph office which with the growing

business could give the community a day and night service throughout the year. That is the present position in many European countries and it has proved to be a great blessing to the people who live at a distance from the centres of population. The Winnipeg ' Free Press ' is making a strong campaign now to improve railway conditions particularly in the west, and it has been able to prove that the people of the west are paying more in freight charges than are the people of the United States, and far more than the people of eastern Canada. The ' Free Press ' shows that if we had an improved parcel post system we would immediately get reduced freight charges all over the Northwest. I give the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' credit for its campaign in that direction. It has made out a case against the railways and express companies and a good way to bring those corporations to time is to extend the parcel post system in this country. The Postmaster General and the ex-Postmaster General are here to-night and I hope they will give us some information on the subject, and I hope that the result of this debate will be that the government will accept the principle I advocated and declare themselves in favour of an extended parcel post. To show what the feeling of the west is I read the following from a speech made in this House by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) a few days ago:
Some time ago the hon, member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux), then Postmaster General, proposed that the parcel post system should be greatly extended. At that time I felt that it was going to he of more use to the departmental stores in our country than to the public in general and I was one of those who told him I would not support that proposition. I must say that I have changed my mind. I think I made a mistake, and those of us, and there were enough of us to stop his good efforts, who voted in that way, did in my opinion make a mistake. T hope the Postmaster General will, unless we get better treatment from the express companies, extend the parcel post system. If the Postmaster General introduces an extended parcel post system I will support him now because we have not had fair treatment from the express companies, and if the express companies want to head off an extended parcel post they will substantially and quickly reduce their rates.
There is no use waiting, or threatening an investigation before tfie Railway Commission, let us declare for an extended parcel post system now, and relief will come at once.
As I have said, I wish to see adopted in this country that new and great principle in connection with private owned public franchises, public competition wherever it can be put in force. Of course I would prefer to see a public monopoly in this matter and not the competition that I propose Mr. MACLEAN (South York).
in this case. But perhaps we are not ready to come to that. I am ready for public ownership of all these monopolies now and completely. I would put the express companies completely out of business, I would take over the whole monopoly. I would put the telegraph companies out of business and make that a government monopoly. But if we cannot have that let us have public competition so as bring down the rates and improve the service.
What is the essential advantage of public ownership over private ownership in the matter of great public utilities? It is this: Public ownership seeks to improve the service and cheapen the price, while private ownership tries to reduce the service and increase the profits of the owners. The difference is as wide as that between daylight and dark, the difference between a corporation, an organization of men trying to improve and widen the service ana cheapen the cost, and an organization of men trying to make the most money possible out of it. Wherever there has been public ownership of these great utilities the result has been to extend the service to a great many people. There is always a line in public ownership where the service does not pay, but year after year such a service is extended to the smaller and outlying communities, thereby increasing its usefulness. But the first thing a private company controlling a public monopoly says is: Is there a big profit in it for us, if not we shall not extend it until you can show us that there is money in it. The whole tendency of the world to-day is to extend the parcel post system. They are coming to it in the United States, they have every faith in it in Great Britain and Europe; they have worked it out in Australia and New Zealand until it is a great-success and why should Canada further delay? Why should somebody be able to come into this House, the railway and express companies, I imagine, and under the guise of protecting the country storekeepers, prevent the people of this country having so useful and necessary a thing as cheap parcel post? The railways should not have that influence and I hope they will not have it any longer. I hope that the members here to-night, irrespective of party, will declare in favour of the extension of a parcel post system and let the word go to the people of the Canadian west to-morrow, in their trials and difficulties and the trouble that has come to them by reason of the late crops, the bad weather and the inability of the railways to give them caTe, and of the elevators to store their grain.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: And the lack of markets.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext:
And the lack of markets, if the hon. gentleman wishes to say so, and bring the political

idea into it. If we can do something for them, let us do it now, let us do something for the people of the west to-day. We are giving them a Grain Act, an important advantage, let us give them something else, let us give them, a cheaper parcel post and cheaper express to-morrow. If we give them cheaper express by parcels post to-morrow, then next week they will have cheaper telegraphs, the railways will see that if they do not reduce their telegraph rates there will be public competition there as well. If we could give them reduced passenger rates, that would be a great relief to them. Our railways are earning enormous profits, and the people in the west should have a cheaper passenger rate. I tried the other night to get an equalization of freight charges in this country. That is something to which they are entitled. [DOT]
I hope the House will unite in support of this motion, and that we will be able to give to the people of the Canadian west an immediate relief in the way of express charges not only in their country, but throughout the whole of Canada.
I therefore beg to move, seconded by Mr. McCraney:
That all the words after ' that ' be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
This House is of the opinion that the expansion and extension of the parcels post system would be in the public interest.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the principle of this motion, and after having heard the last remarks of the hon. member for South York, I am even more strongly in favour of it because the hon. gentleman by his remarks has gone a little further than the words of his motion. He is not only in favour of an extension of the parcel post system, but also in favor of larger markets for the Canadian farmer.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext:
And when I hear such a doughty supporter of protection as he was during the last general election advocating larger markets for the Canadian farmer, surely I cannot be false to the motion which he has so ably presented to the House.
My hon. friend has .appealed to me as a former Postmaster General, and has been kind enough to quote some remarks which I made last year on the subject when I had the^ honour of being Postmaster General. It is true that last year, speaking on this very question, I expressed the opinion very frankly and speaking for myself alone, that the day was not far distant when the Post Office Department of Canada should take upon itself the duty of establishing a parcel post system. At the present the parcel post service is chiefly carried on by the railway companies, or by the express companies, the Canadian Express Company, and the Dominion Express Company, which are part and parcel of the two great railway systems, the Canadian Pacific railway, and the Grand Trunk railway. In every European country the express business is carried on by the Post Office Department.
Allow me to express here the opinion which I expressed the other day before the Canadian Club of Montreal, and which was re-echoed by the press, that the day has practically come in Canada when the Postmaster General should be not only the letter carrier of His Majesty the King, but should also be (as he is in foreign countries) the minister of communication. In England, in France, in Germany, in Japan, and very soon to be in the United States the Postmaster General is the superintendent not only of the post office, but also of the telegraph and telephone rates and parcel post system.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that we have in our post office regulations a parcel post system in the embryonic stage. It is hidden in the Canadian Official Postal Guide. My hon. friend the Postmaster General, in whose ability and alertness and businesslike methods I have the utmost confidence, will see himself that we are only at the embryonic stage-that for many reasons, which he knows as well as I do, the express companies were allowed to hold in their hands the parcel post system of this country. However, notwithstanding the regulations of his department, the time has come when a bold policy should be adopted and when the Post Office Department-should establish a popular and cheap parcel post such as they have in other countries of the old world, even in japan.
I might remind my hon. friend that some years ago when I took office there was a movement on foot, especially in the province of Ontario, and in some of the provinces of the west, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, strongly in favour of the establishment of a cheap parcel post system in Canada. I received many petitions praying for the establishment of such a system, but, concurrently or concomitantly I was deluged with petitions signed by farmers who were deluded into signing'them by the railway companies. It was easy to see" that these petitions were engineered by the railway companies, or rather by the express companies. My hon. friend the Postmaster General may see these petitions in the Post Office Department. They are in the archives of the department, if they have not been eaten by the rats. He will see that whether these petitions were signed in the province of Ontario or in the constituencies of the west they were all worded in about

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: Not ours.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: No, but my hon. friend remembers when we had to pay 3 cents on a letter.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: Five cents.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext:
Until 1893 our cheapest rate was 3 cents. The- penny system was then adopted as between Canada and the
rest of the empire. There were people who predicted a huge deficit in the Post Office Department. On the contrary, I make bold to say, the surplus of the post office is due directly to the reduction of the postal rates. Some years ago, I myself as Postmaster General, introduced a reduction in the rates on what are called ' drop letters/ letters to addresses in the city within which they are posted. This was a reduction from two cents to one cent on a letter and applied to all the large cities of the country. I was told by the officers of the department that we might perhaps suffer a check for some years in the revenue of the department. On the contrary, within a few months after the rate of 1 cent for drop, letters had been adopted, we had a surplus, a surplus which must be attributed to the fact that we reduced the rates. And the same result will follow if my hon. friend will adopt cheap parcel post for this country. In postal matters the United States has been a follower of Canada, having followed us in the adoption of many improvements which we ourselves had borrowed from Great Britain. For instance, there was the postal savings bank system, which, copied from Canada by the United States, has been a great success. But as regards the parcel post, the United States has stolen a march on Canada. I have here a report, the latest issue that they have in the library. That report shows that Postmaster General Hitchcock has proposed to establish a cheap parcel post, using in that connection, the agency of the rural mail system.
I read from page 10 of the Post Office Department Annual Reports of the United States:
The recommendation made in the last annual report of the department for the introduction of a limited parcel post service on rural routes is earnestly renewed. It is believed that as soon as the postal savings system is thoroughly organized the Post Office Department should be prepared to establish throughout the country a general parcel post. As the preliminary step in the development of such a -service it is hoped, that Congress will authorize the delivery on rural routes of parcels weighing as much as 11 pounds-
Our limit is 5 pounds.
-which is the weight limit for the international parcel post. This form of service can be conducted with little, if any, additional expense to the government. It will not require the appointment of more carriers, for those already employed have the necessary equipment in the way of horses and wagons to distribute the parcels as welt -as the ordinary mail, which is rarely of sufficient volume to take up more -than a small portion of the mail space in the carrier's wagon. A rural parcel post of the kind proposed, if successfully conducted, would probably lead to a. more general system. Before the parcel ser-

vice is extended to the whole country, however, definite information should be obtained as to the nature and volume of the business (o be handled. It is accordingly urged that in conjunction with the experiment on rural routes a further inquiry be authorized by Congress in order that the department may be in a better position to develop the system on conservative lines and that a special appropriation for the inquiry be promptly granted.
This was in 1910, and since then the United States Post Office Department have put in force a limited parcel post system in connection with the rural mail system. Now I would not be so radical as to say that throughout the whole length and breadth of Canada there should be a general parcel post system, at very low rates. The machinery for such a system would be very costly to . begin with, and I do not know whether it would work very well. You can require the rural mail carrier to carry a parcel, because he has the machinery for it; but the ordinary mail carrier, where there is no rural mail delivery, is not in the same position. Of course, the hon. gentleman would have to invite new tenders, and to revise many of his contracts. I am aware that he is revising some of them without establishing a parcel post. However, that is only en passant. The hon. gentleman will see at once that by extending his rural mail system, although limited in its extent, which he has at present, he can start in with a cheap parcel post. I know that my hon. friend will be opposed at the start, but opposed by whom? Not by the people of this country, not by the honest merchants, butj he will W opposed by the express companies. But the express companies have taken out of our hands the business which we ought to ehrry ourselves. The parcel post is one of the public utilities which by its nature pertain to the Postmaster General.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: Did the hon. gentleman find any opposition to the parcel post system by the country merchants?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext:
I explained a moment ago that when I took office there was for a time a strong agitation in the press of the country generally in favour of a cheap parcel post. When petitions began to pour in to the department, I was surprised to find that all those petitions were worded in the same way, the same reasons were invoked against the system, in fact the same printed forms were used all over Canada. _ From what I gathered from the officers in the department, I concluded in my own mind that the agitation originated from the express companies; in fact I have no doubt of it whatever. That is easy to understand. The moment the Postmaster General of Canada starts a Mr. LEMIEUX.
cheap parcel post system, having already under his hand a complete machinery to carry it out, it is easy to understand that his rivals will be the express companies. But I say again, the express companies ought not. to be allowed to take away from the Postmaster General a business which by its nature pertains to his department. At all events, the establishment of a cheap parcel post system would bring the express companies to reason and to terms. Let me read from a pamphlet published by Mr. Kindel, ' Relation of a Parcel Post to Businessmen and Farmers'; this was read, before the Trans-Mississippi Congress in November, 1911. Here is a paragraph which applies exactly to our own conditions in Canada; in fact, you might change the names of the cities of New York and Boston to Montreal and Toronto, and you will find that it exactly describes our conditions:
How the United States government discriminates against its own citizens in favour of those of foreign countries.
Well, my hon. friend and myself, unwillingly, when I was in office, did discriminate against our own citizens in favour of those of foreign countries.
To illustrate the inconsistency in connection with the parcel post service attention is drawn to the following conditions: An individual entering any post office in the United States with two parcels weighing four pounds each will be obliged to pay 64 cents on the one to New York, for example, while for the one destined to a foreign country, although it usually passes through New York city, the charge is 48 cents. Should the weight be 4 pounds 6 ounces, a package addressed to the resident of New York will be denied admission to the mail by the postmaster, while the package intended for a resident of a foreign land wilt be accepted and forwarded, probably via New York, at the rate of 12 cents per pound. The parcels for the foreign country will be received in most instances up to 11 pounds. In other words, our own people must pay 4 cents per pound more for the privilege of dispatching packages to each other than when destined to residents of foreign countries.
I have already said that when I was Postmaster General-I make no bones about it, my hon. friend and myself are equally guilty in that respect-we have been too kind to the express companies, and we have not been bold enough in regard to a parcel post in former years. We should have been as bold in this direction as we have been in the reduction of postal rates on letters and drop letters. Let me read to the House a paragraph from ' La Follette's Weekly ':
At present, the transportation of parcels, except for very small ones, is in the grip of the express monopoly. Every person who sends a Christmas package must pay tribute to the few individuals who control the express

business-must help to create those enormous 24 million dollar ' lemons/ Service that is rightly part of the people's Post Office Department is now performed not as a public function but as a means of building up col-lossal private fortunes.
If the Christmas package were our only small parcels transportation problem, it would not be serious. But, as a nation, the shipment of parcels enters in an important degree into the economy of our daily life. Now to send small shipments quickly, cheaply, and securely is a thing which America has apparently been unable to learn from the enlightened countries of Europe, Australia, Asia, Africa and South America. It is not that the people of the country do not understand the condition, nor that they do not Understand the remedy. It i9 only that congress is deaf to the public demands for a national parcels post.
Here is a good occasion for my hon. friend to make a name for himself. I will give him all the credit he will deserve if he starts, in the not too far distant future, a cheap parcel post system.
Representative agencies of public thought, neswspap-ers and public speakers have for years voiced this demand. Labour organizations in their national conventions and through their accredited representatives, have emphasised it. The farmers of the country plead for it.
But for some mysterious reason the demand, not only of the farmers but of labouring men and public spirited oitizens generally, when they have touched the subject of parcels post have been persistently ignored by congress.
A parcel post is no mysterious thing. It means simply that congress shall authorize and that the Post Office Department shall put into operation rules and machinery for the transportation of packages in the domestic mails of the United States reasonable rates, subject only to reasonable, not arbitrary limitation as to size and weight.
As I stated a moment ago, you can 'substitute the words ' parliament of Canada,' for ' Congress,' and the name ' Ottawa ' for ' New York,' and you have exactly a picture of our parcel post system as it at present exists in Canada. If my hon.friend wishes seriously and conscientiously to deal with this subject, I warn him at once that he will meet with some obstacles in his path.	I mentioned a
moment ago the express companies. He may also meet with some red tape in the department. I do not wish to blame the officials of the department, but I only wish to say that after a system has been in existence for years and after certain rates have been established, strange to say, when a demand is made for a reduction or a change immediately objections are made, not by the public, not by legislators, but by the officials of the department. In the Post, Office Department I can say that my hon. friend has most, intelligent officers who are quite in
accord with the public on his question. I would remind him of one thing.. If it is not shelved, he will find a report in the department on this very question prepared by my good friend, Mr. Geo. Ross, of Toronto, chief Postoffice Superintendent of Canada, one of the ablest men in the world as regards postal matters generally. I would not be afraid to put Mr. Geo. Ross of Toronto on a par with the postoffice officials of any country in the world. He has been trained in the postoffice system for forty years. He is a very able man, full of ideas and always ready to accept a reform when a reform suggests itself to the public. My hon. friend will find in the del partment a very lengthy report prepared by Mr. Ross about three months ago. I was under the charm of that report when I left office, unfortunately. That report simply confirms what my hon. friend has stated this evening and very largely what the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) stated yesterday. If my hon. friend will read the remarks made by my hon. friend for East Lambton yesterday-I am sorry I cannot refer to a past debate- he will find concrete facts which are corroborated by Mr. Ross in his lengthy and able report which conclusively proves the necessity of starting afresh on this question of the parcel post in Canada. Now, I have said all I have to say on this question.

speechtext: I desire to profit by the experience which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux), has had while occupying the high position of Postmaster General for several years, and perhaps he will be prepared to give some suggestions as to how this parcels post system might be put into effect as far as rates and weights are concerned.

speechtext: My hon. friend will find all that in Mr. Ross' report.

speechtext: I want to know if my hon. friend agrees with those figures, because I have seen the report.

speechtext: If my hon. friend has seen the report I am very glad because he is more conversant with the subject than I thought he was. I agree completely with Mr. Ross' conclusions, and I say that the hon. member for East Lambton yesterday propounded a scheme which could be arranged. By your leave, Mr. Speaker, I might be allowed to quote a few of the remarks of the hon. member for East Lambton. .

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: This is part of the subject introduced by the hon. member for East Lambton, and discussed yesterday. While great latitude is allowed in moving an amendment to go into Committee of Supply, there is a limitation to it which I think it is well to keep in mind.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: There is no objection whatever on this side of the House to the hon. gentleman going into this subject fully. It is a matter of very great public interest.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) illustrated yesterday the way in which the system, as propounded by Mr. Ross, could be worked out in Canada, and how it vyould be possible to do away with the objection raised wfith respect to departmental stores. It is a scheme which would establish the parcels post system within the limits of rural mail routes, and would not deprive the country merchants of their clientele. My hon. friend will, I am sure, read over the report of Mr. Ross. I fully agree with that report. I have nothing more to add on this subject. I am in accord with the motion made by the hon. member for South York, In this matter, as in all matters, it requires a little boldness and some courage. We have been experimenting in the Post Office Department for the last ten or fifteen years with this result, as the logical conclusion of these experiments, that whenever we have * established cheap rates we have had larger revenues. The same thing is true with respect to cables. Some years ago when there was but one cable between America and Europe the rate for one word was fl, and the cable service was, therefore, inaccessible to the people.
The moment a second company was started there was a reduction in the rates, in 1887 and 1888 the cable rates, because of competition went dow'n so low as twelve cents a word. So long as the express companies are not interfered with there will be a monopoly and high express rates, but if the Postmaster General follows the suggestions made by Mr. Ross in his very able report, he will render a great service not only to the residents of the cities, but to the farmers of the country as well. In Germany and France the farmers make tremendous use of the parcel post system by sending their staples such as eggs, butter and cheese to the market, and the parcel post is one of the paying agencies of the postal service in European countries. Great Britain is in the van of progress amongst all civilized nations in her postal service. From Great Britain we got the penny post, and let us copy her in the parcel post system. Later on we can have a cheap telegraphic communication by establishing a state-owned cable between Canada and the mother country. If the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) does all that he will make a great name for himself.
Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.) I hope my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) will be able to show us, as he has said, that the introduction of this parcel post system will Mr. SPEAKER:.
not unduly advantage the departmental stores of the cities, and unduly disadvantage the country merchants.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: I trust the Postmaster General will place before the House the report of Mr. Ross which shows that a local parcel post system such as they have in the United States can be established without injuring the country merchant, but rather that it will be an advantage to him. I know that a great objection comes from the country merchant, but the country merchant is stirred up insidiously by the express companies, and the objection is in reality only fictitious. We all know the methods of the monopolies for years and years in this country. On this important question which is now so widely discussed, my hon. friend will find that the report of Mr. Ross demonstrates that a local parcel post system will work to the advantage of the country merchant.

The ancient constitutional doctrine that the redress of grievances is to he considered before the granting of supplies, is now represented by the practice of permitting every description of amendment to be moved on the question for the Speaker leaving the chair before going into the Committee of Supply or Ways and Means.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext:
I wish to second the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) and to give a few reasons why I wish to see the extension of the parcel post service. Those who have followed the discussion in the public press know that there is discrimination against the west in the matter of express rates. A rate which in the eastern provinces would be say $1, would be about $1.66 in the west. An extension of the parcel post system which would to a great extent do the business of the express companies would do away with that discrimination against the west.
Another grievance which our people in the west have is the paying of double express rates. The recipient of a parcel by express from Ontario who resides on the line of the Canadian Northern railway must pay an express rate to each of the two companies-The Dominion Express Company and the Canadian Northern Railway Express Company-during the winter season. There is no more reason for charging two express rates on an express parcel than for charging double postage on a letter going into any part of the west. An extension of the parcel post system would remove that double charge. Another reason for supporting this motion is that the express rates are too high and that the business if taken over by the government could be administered more economically than it is by the express companies and the exorbitant charges would be wiped out.
I was pleased to hear the remarks of my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) with regard to the country storekeeper. I have not yet got away from the idea that
the country storekeeper is the mainstay of the settler. In the west many of our people who are poor, have no money and have no means of getting out their wheat and so must get credit. They do not get credit from T. Eaton & Company or from Robert Simpson & Company. It is the country storekeeper who must keep these people alive until they are able to get cash. If some arrangement can be worked out which will produce a system of parcel post which will not be to the disadvantage of the country storekeeper, then we will have a very perfect system indeed and when my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) with all his experience, assures us that that can be done, I am very glad indeed to support the proposal which is before the House.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: I am heartily in favour of the motion before the House. My principal reason is that the express companies are so exorbitant in their charges on goods going to the west. For instance I have in my office a bill for a four pound box of candy that was sent from Ottawa to Edmonton a year ago last Christmas. The box cost $2.40, and the Canadian Pacific railway express company charged $2.50 to take it from here to Edmonton. That has been the whole trouble, and I do not know of any better way to bring the express companies to time than to extend the parcel post. I would not like to interfere with the country merchants but I believe, as the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), has said that a system can be devised that will be fair to the country merchants and to the settlers as well. We must always bear in mind that for one country merchant there are 50 farmers or more, so that their interests, I think, have to be kept well to the fore. The express charges are simply ruinous and this is the best way to deal with them.

M.r. BLAIN. Was it carried by one express company or two?

1 was very much interested in the speech of the ex-Postmaster General, more especially with reference to the effect produced by the reduction of rates

of postage, particularly on drop letters. subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.

speechtext: His argument then was that he could not make up his mind to give the people in the small towns and villages and in the townships a reduction to one-half cent on drop letters in rural districts until he had discovered what would be the result of the drop from two cents to one cent in the cities. subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE PARCEL POST SYSTEM.
speechtext: Hear, hear, the time has come now.
