On section 82: grain of same grade to be kept together; certificate for mixed cargo.

As a representative of the district in which the terminal elevators are situated, I would like to say a few words in connection with clause 82. The question of mixing grades has been a live issue both in the United States and Canada for the past twenty years.	The
United States have solved this question by allowing mixing in the terminal elevators. In Canada there seems to be an opinion that mixing is a crime. It is a misdemeanour, and a civil offence according to our law, but I want you to look at this, Mr. Chairman, as a simple business pro-Mr. OLIVER.
position, and it is from that standpoint that I purpose saying a few words with regard to it. The process of mixing, as I understand it, is simply raising up to a certain grade a class of wheat which, through climatic conditions, has suffered deterioration, by mixing with it another grade of wheat which has a superabundance over and above what the law requires of those qualities in which the first sample is deficient. I will give an illustration. We will take a car of Wheat which is No. I Northern in every way, except with respect to Red Fife wheat. The law requires that there shall be sixty per cent of Red Fife wheat. If that car had only 55 per cent of red fife wheat it is graded as No. 2. We will take another car which has all the qualifications of No. 2 Northern, but has only forty per cent instead of forty-five iper cent of Red Fife wheat, which, therefore, is graded No. 3. I will take these two cars and mix them. I fulfil the requirements of No. 2 grade; that is I raise up a No. 3 car to No. 2. The average spread in the price between the two grades is 5 cents per bushel. On 1,000 bushels I would make $50. At the present time there is a difference of about 7 cents between No. 2 and No. 3 Northern, so that in that case I would make a little more. But, take another instance. Take a car that is all Red Fife wheat, but has been frosted. It will not be graded as No. 1, but as No. 2. Then I can take seven other cars that are No. 2 in every respect, but have only got 40 per cent of Red Fife instead of 45. I will take these eight cars, mix them, and I will have what will pass inspection as No. 2 grade. Thus, by using one car I can raise the whole seven cars to No. 2 grade. Otherwise, the whole seven cars would, under our law, be graded as No. 3. There is a profit of 5 cents a bushel on 7,000 bushels, or $350.
We had an instance at Port Arthur the other day where a car of flax was shipped to Mr. Irwin of the Consolidated Elevator. That flax was one pound short in weight per bushel. It was shipped as No. 1. The owner thought that he would get No. 1 grade, but when it was inspected it was graded. as rejected. There is a difference of 25 cents a bushel between No. 1 and rejected and he applied to the survey board in Winnipeg, but they maintained the inspection. He wired down to Mr. Irwin at the Consolidated Elevator to ship the flax to Duluth, because he could get practically the full! difference in price between the two grades there or about 25 cents a bushel more, for the car. But the car had been unloaded. I maintain that there is a great economic loss to the farmers of Canada, because mixing is not allowed. I believe that there is between $4,000,000 and $5,000,000 a year lost to the

farmers of this country under the system which has hitherto prevailed, and will be lost under the proposal contained in the present Bill.
Would my hon. friend not rather say that this is lost to the dealers and not to the farmers?

No, the farmer is the man who will get it. 1 am glad that question was asked, because it brings up another point in connection with mixing which 1 shall take up in a moment. Now,
I would like to ask why was mixing prohibited? You will remember that under the old system the elevator man bought on his own account, and also stored the grain for tlie public. He took the fat grades of the public, mixed them with his own wheat and made for himself this extra profit. The farmers objected to it, and legislation was brought in, first, to prohibit the terminal elevator man from dealing in grain and, second, to prevent mixing. I wish to ask this question: Has this law been enforced or can it be enforced? I say that the law has not been enforced, and that it cannot be enforced. As the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), said yesterday in the House, under the system of interlocking directorates, the terminal elevator owmers at the present time are directors of country elevators, and they are buying grain. I will just quote from page 18 of the report of the Select Committee on Bill Q before the Senate, Mr. Searle's testimony. With regard to the elevator at Port Arthur the question was asked:
How many Canadian companies do tlie Pea-vey people control?-A. Do you mean line railways?
Q. Yes.-A. They control the Port Arthur Elevator Company, the British American Elevator Company, the National Elevator Company.
According to a statement with regard to licensed elevators and warehouses, as made out by this government, the British American Elevator Company control 93 elevators -Manitoba 17; Saskatchewan 69; and Alberta 7. These same directors can, and do, buy grain at the present time. Therefore, I maintain that the law has not been enforced. Then the examination proceeds with regard to mixing. We have proof that mixing is going on and I will again read to the committee from page 126 of the Select Committee report on Bill Q. This is evidence in connection with a couple of cases that came up in Port Arthur and Fort William last year in regard to mixing. I shall quote from the testimony of Mr. C. B. Watts, secretary of the Dominion Millers' Association:
At the close of navigation in 1910 we find that Inspector Gibbs at Port Arthur reports 76

to the warehouseman that he finds certain elevators there have shipped out large quantities of No. 1 Northern, and they are short quantities of No. 2 Northern. Now, I do not want to take up the time of the committee, but 1 must refer you to a short extract from Mr. Castle's report of this trial, which these gentlemen say was only a mistake, and it was immaterial, on the enormous quantity of grain handled. The fines imposed by the magistrates show it was not very trivial, as they were $2,500 in one case, and $3,000 in another. Mr. Castle, in his report, says: 'In the Port Arthur elevator the shipments exceeded the receipts of No. 2 Northern by 169,066 bushels. Of the Empire elevator he says the shipments of No. 1 Northern exceeded- the receipts by 137,881 bushels.
It may be said that this is an isolated case in connection with mixing, but I would point out that the government inspectors were on the spot and that they gave an inspection certificate when the grain went in and when it came out. These cases we know of, but I am quite sure there were a great many more where mixing was done and where fines were not imposed. What is the use of putting a law on the statue-books if we icannot enforce it. The purport -of this Bill should be to remove the incentive for wrongdoing and then the wrong will not be done. Under the present law 'the government allows mixing by compelling the elevator man to mix the fat and the lean shipments of any one grade. For instance, in No. 1 Northern you can mix anything that has got sixty per cent Red Fife wheat and up to seventy-five per cent Rred Fife and in No. 2 you can mix the different lean and fat grades of from forty-five to sixty per cent Red Fife. We therefore, allow mixing to-day with certain restrictions and I maintain it would be much better for the country if these restrictions were taken off. I do not wish to see the integrity of our grain destroyed. I do not wish to see our grades lowered and I do not believe they will be lowered by mixing because any shipment of grain that goes out will have to stand the government inspection. The men who get the benefit of the grades to-day are the millers and the European buyers. The miller does not want a sample market. He wants to buy on grades because he is getting a litlle more than he pays for and it is the same with the European buyer. Our samples of grades are sent over t-o the old country and the European buyer buys just on that sample, hoping no doubt that he is going to get a little more than he pays for. The purchaser in the European market buys on the minimum grade and on that point I cite the evidence given by Mr. E. R. Wyland, a large exporter, and which appears on page 160 of the report of the select committee:
The old country man does not buy your wheat on a 64 or 63 pounds to the bushel. He

buys it as 60 pounds to the bushel. That is No. 1 Northern. He buys it on the standard that Mr. Horn and Mr. Gibbs send to the old country market to represent No. 1 Northern. If they get wheat higher than that standard, we get no benefit from that. That is an absolute fact, and any gentleman who has been in the export business knows that the old country buyer will not pay any more for No 1 Northern wheat. '
At page 168 of the same report we find this:
By hon. Mr. Louglieed:
Q. You have stated that the Liverpool price of wheat, or the Liverpool quotation is based on the minimum grade?-A. Yes.
Q. Not on the maximum?-A. Not on the maximum grade.
Let me ask why sliould the question of sentiment enter into the price. I do not know of any other business that is conducted on an economic basis where it is thought that sentiment must be taken into consideration in fixing the price of an article. The European buyer buys on the minimum of the grade and why should our farmers sell on the maximum of that grade? I believe in maintaining the integrity of the high stadards of our grain, but I find in the ' Weekly Report ' issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce for January 29 last year, that the shipment of Canadian wheat alone through United States channels amounted to 33,806,535 bushels last year. That wheat goes through with our government certificate, but when it goes into the American elevator we lose absolute control of it. A few weeks ago a shipment of No. 2 Northern was rejected in the old country because there was a great deal of corn mixed with it, and everyone knows we do not grow any corn in Manitoba. We have no control over that grain when it goes through the United States elevators and yet a most important thing for the farmer of the west is to maintain the identity and integrity of Canadian grain. I want to see that our gram shall always maintain its present high standing, but we certainly cannot keen control of it when it passes through United States channels. I think I have shown that the terminal elevator interests are violating the law and do buy grain.
Does the certificate have any existence when the wheat goes into a foreign country?
If it is shipped through in bond the Canadian certificate will remain with that wheat and it is sold in the old country on that certificate.
No.
The hon. member (Mr. Carrick) is right.

I did not say that. We were talking of selling on a sample and selling on a sample market. What I said was that millions of bushels were sold on sample and not on certificate; that when certificates were granted they could be thrown away and the farmer could sell on the sample. But we have no sample market, of course.

I stand corrected, but I understood the attitude of some hon. gentlemen opposite to be that the farmer sold his grain on sampie and not on grade I believe the farmer does not sell anything on sample. The track buyer, who is an expert, has his samples of all grades before him when he buys. A car of grain may be No. 1 in everything except perhaps colour, hardness, size or Red Fife, and may fall down a little in one of these qualifications. It is graded No. 2 by the buyer and the farmer is paid only for No. 2. He does not get any benefit whatever from the spreads, and we all know that there is a great difference in the value of the different grades. I have here a few quotations from the 'Grain Growers' Guide' of November 8, 1911, which show that No. 1 Northern wheat on a sample market sold on one day as low as $1.02 and as high as $1,061, other

cars selling at $1.04, $1.05$ and $1.05}. On the same day No. 2 sold at as low as 99 cents and as high as $1.04. I have also the quotations of the Minneapolis sample market of November 4, as printed in the ' Grain Growers' Guide ' of November 8 showing that barley No. 4, sold as follows; one car, at $1.03, three at $1.13, one at $1.11 and one at $1.14. There was a difference of 11 cents for tlie same grade on the same day. I maintain that the only man who loses the value of these spreads is the farmer. Now who gets the benefit of the spreads? The millers and the European buyers. We allow the millers to blend wheat; why do we not allow the farmers and the elevator men to mix it? The miller can blend the different grades and sell the different brands of flour in the open market; but there is a restriction placed upon all other owners in regard to the mixing of grain I eontnd to the detriment of the farmer. Now, the farmers have asked for a sample market, but a sample market is not workable unless mixing prevails. On this point I would like to quote from the ' Grain Growers' Guide,' of January 3, page 16. I understand that this is the great farmers' paper in the western country. This is an article by F. W. Eva, who is the chief grain inspector for the state of Minnesota, in which he says:
Should the Winnipeg market decide to make a sample market they certainly will have to permit the mixing of grain in elevators; the two go together. The intermingling or mixing of grain of different grades, resulting in improving of low grades to a higher grade, is considered by all grain men and handlers as legitimate a business as the improving or mixing of any article in any other line of business. The mixing of wheat does not injure the producer, but as a matter of fact, is a benefit, as is well known by all conversant with the grain business. It increases the number of buyers, creates competition and results in a premium above the price of the regular grade for the choice lots of cars in each grade. No prominent market in the United States is without these facilities.
If a sample market is to be established, there is only one place for it, that is, at the head of Canadian navigation. The modus onerandi of the sample market at Minneapolis is this:	About one hundred miles
from that city samples are taken from the car and are sent by express to Minneapolis, and by the time the car arrives the grain is sold on these samnles. We can do the samp thing jn flip handling of our western grain. We can establish a sample market either at Port Arthur or Fort William.
Which would the hon. member prefer?

I would rather not ai s-wer that question, as 1 represent both citie* Samples could be forwarded to the 76$
sample market by express, and the grain would arrive three or four days later. There would thus be an opportunity of disposing' of the grain before its arrival, so that there would be no delay in its transportation. The solution I offer, then, for the situation is: first, that we should have a sample market at the head of navigation; second, that mixing be allowed; third, that we should have two systems of terminal elevators-public elevators operated by railways, with mixing prohibited, and private elevators to handle only their own grain, but to be allowed to mix. If the farmer wants to send his grain to the old country, he can store it in the public elevator, where there is no mixing, so that the grain keeps its integrity; while if he bqjieves he will get a little more for it if it is mixed, he -can send it or sell it to the private elevator.
Would you allow the grain which goes to the mixing elevator to be inspected and graded out?

Yes, that is my whole argument. The government have their inspectors there, and after the grain is mixed it must come up to the high standard demanded by this government. It is claimed now that the Manitoba grain brings more money than the American, and why should it not? What qualifications are required on the other side for No. 1 N'vr*v,prT'p Take the requirements for the American No. 1 Northern. That grade requires only 50 per cent of hard wheat and a weight of 57 pounds to the bushel. What is our No

The commissioner shall have power in his discretion to order cars to be supplied, contrary to the provisions of the Act, to elevators that are in danger of collapse, or in cases where the operator of any country elevator reports in writing under oath that some portion of the grain in his elevator or warehouse is heated, and that in order to preserve the same it is necessary to ship such heated grain to the terminal elevator for treatment: provided, however, that no relief shall be granted in such last mentioned cases as long as the warehouseman has plenty of room in his building for the rehandling of such grain.
The condition of things at the present time, as I stated is very onerous and may be productive of great loss unless the conditions be met as rapidly and effectively as possible. I am going to ask the House, if no one objects, to allow me to introduce an amendment to that section of the Act and to put it through its different stages, to this effect: That after the word 'collapse ' in the third line, there be inserted ' all places where grain is damp and liable to become damp, or for the purpose of distributing seed grain to any point in the western division.' In these cases the ware-, houseman shall have the same option and discretion as is given him in the other two eases. All the representatives of the different interests, including the railways, are
favourable to this being done. And I might say that the Board of Railway Commissioners have also recommended it. I move that the rules relating to this matter be suspended and that leave be given to introduce this Bill.

Motion agreed to.

The object of the Bill to be founded on this resolution is to enable the government to advance a further sum of $6,000,000 to the Montreal Harbour Commissioners for the purpose of developing that port. 1.	New high level quays, (having an aggregate frontage of 16,800,000 feet) so arranged as to give 24 new ocean berths for vessels of from 600 to 800 feet.

Mr. Speaker, on this motion I desire to direct

the attention of the government, and of the House generally to a matter which I think is of the very greatest importance, and to which I had occasion to refer at an earlier period in the session, when I had the honour of moving for all the papers in regard to imperial naturalization, and the communications that passed between the home government and this government with reference to the passing of a measure which would enable persons who are naturalized in Canada to become in truth and verity citizens of the British Empire, as under the existing laws they are not. As a result of the motion I then made, a return has been brought down, which I have before me, and which shows that following upon the proceedings of the Imperial Conference, which were discussed on the occasion of that motion, the imperial authorities prepared, to be sent to each of the self-governing colonies, a draft Bill dealing with this question; and they desire to receive from each of these colonies its approval of the measure in order that it may be passed by the imperial parliament, and that legislation of a subsidiary character may also be passed, in the various colonies in order to remove the difficulty. That Bill was sent to this government during the past summer. The home government apparently acted very promptly after the action of the Imperial Conference in proceeding with the draft measure. In brief, that measure provides for a complete change in the naturalization laws of the empire. It purports in its first clause to define natural-born British subjects. The language used in the [DOT]beginning of that section is as follows:
The following persons shall he deemed to he naturalized British subjects.
It then goes on to define those born within His Majesty's allegiance, and certain other classes of persons who are said to be naturalized British subjects. I think this must be a mistake in the Bill for natural-horn British subjects. The second section provides for the Secretary of State granting a certificate of naturalization to an alien who makes an application for the purpose, and satisfies the Secretary of State that he has resided for a period of five years in His Majesty's dominions, or has been in the service of the Crown for not less than five years within the last eight years before the application. The use of the phrase ' His Majesty's dominions ' makes this a wider provision than that of the present law, which requires that residence must have been within the United Kingdom. The second requirement is that the applicant is of good character and has adequate knowledge of the English language. There are certain other provisions in that section which are not particularly apropos to this discussion. Then, the 77*
certificate of naturalization is not to take effect until the applicant has taken the oath of allegiance. This is an outline of the principles on which it is proposed that the naturalization may be granted-five years residence in any of His Majesty's dominions or five years in the service of the Crown, not necessarily within those dominions; that the applicant should, be of good character and have an adequate knowledge of the English language, . and that the oath of allegiance should be taken. If that section were passed by the imperial parliament-though it seems to me there might be some improvement in the drafting-it would be open to any person who had resided in Canada for that period to make application to the British Secretary of State for imperial naturalization. There is a provision later on which enables each one of the colonial governments to grant a certificate. But before coming to that I would take the sections in their order. A most material one, which applies to the certificate granted by any of the governments, is worthy of consideration. It provides:
A person to whom a certificate of naturalization is granted by a Secretary of State, shall, subject to tlie provisions of this Act, be entitled to all political and other rights, powers and privileges, and be subject to all obligations, duties and liabilities to which a natural-born British subject is entitled and, as from the date of his naturalization, have to all intents and purposes the status of a natural-born British subject.
That section is a new one and is very wide in its effect. It practically creates the Imperial naturalization of aliens. There are other provisions with reference to peculiar cases, such as the Secretary of State granting a certificate in the case of doubt as to naturalization, or where a person has previously obtained a certificate of naturalization, power is given to the Secretary of State to grant a new one having a wider effect. Then, section 7 gives power to the Colonies as follows:
The government of any British possession shall have the same power to grant a certificate of naturalization as the Secretary of State has under this Act, and the provisions of this Act as to the grant and revocation of such a certificate shall apply accordingly, with the substitution of the government of the possession for the Secretary of .State, and the possession for the United Kingdom, and also, in a possession where any language is recognized as on an equality with the English language, with the substitution of that language for the English language.
I hope that the government, in looking into this Act, will give special attention to this clause, which is a vital one so far as this colony is concerned, and there ought to be no doubt about the colony's right which is intended to be created. The
m:

sight which is supposed to be conferred upon each one of the colonial governments is one which cannot be exercised until certain things are done:
This section shall not take effect in any of *the dominions specified in the first schedule to this Act unless the legislature of that dominion adopt the section.
'Then there is this general clause which also makes wide and clear the power of the colonial governments:
Any certificate of naturalization granted under this section shall have the same effect as a certificate of naturalization granted by the 'Secretary of State under this Act in all parts [DOT]of His Majesty's dominions other than a dominion as defined by this Act, the legislature of which has not adopted this section.
The right of the colonial legislatures or parliaments to deal with the question of the exclusion of aliens or British subjects is preserved under this proposed Act in the following clause:
Nothing in this Act shall take away or -abridge any power vested in or exerciseable by the legislature or government of any British possession or prevent any such legislature or government from treating differently different classes of British subjects.
That would, of course, reserve the Tight to Canada to discriminate against Hindus or any other class of British subjects if this colonial parliament desire to *do so. Then there is the validity of statutes that may be passed by the parliaments-I notice the word * legislature ' is used by the drafter at home which is not the apt word either here or in Australia, although I suppose the word may be used in some other colonies. This section says:
All laws, statutes and ordinances made by irbe legislature of a British possession for imparting to any person any of the privileges [DOT]of naturalization to be enjoyed by him with-:in the limits of that possession shall within 'those limits have the authority of law, but -subject to be confirmed or disallowed by His Majesty.
That preserves to the parliament of 'Canada, of which we are speaking more particularly now, the right to continue the naturalization of aliens by the granting of a limited certificate which would not be of as full effect as those which were granted under the Imperial laws. We grant certificates of naturalization in Canada on three years residence; the right to continue to do that would be preserved by this Act, but two years more of residence *would be necessary as supplementary in order to entitle them to the wider certificate.
This Act, which was drafted by home authorities, was the product of the proceedings of the Imperial Conference and Mr. MACDONALD.
the understanding arrived at in a general way by representatives of the selfgoverning dominions there with the Colonial Secretary who made an attempt to prepare a Bili that would be satisfactory to all the self-governing colonies as well as to the home authorities. This Bill has been submitted to all the colonies and has been approved of by the government of South Africa, as appears by letter of Mr. Harcourt, dated November 18, 1911, in which he communicates to the Governor General the fact that, he had received a telegram from the Governor General of the Union of South Africa, on the subject of the Draft Imperial British Nationality and Status of Aliens Bill, and asking that the Canadian ministers should forward their views on the Draft Bill at an early date. The telegram from South Africa is as follows:
November 2, 1911.
Tour despatch 14th July, naturalization Bill, ministers state that objections raised by government of union South Africa in this matter are fairly met by the new draft and they have no alterations to propose.- Gladstone.
The result is that the matter is now before the government for consideration here and it is desirable that at as early a date as possible the government should take steps to deal with the question and be prepared to advise the home authorities as to whether the provisions of this Bill are satisfactory or not or what alterations or amendments they would suggest.
Time, I think, is an object in regard to this matter. The discussion upon this question has gone on in an academic way for something like the last ten years. I do not pretend to say that there is a very strong public opinion upon the question in Canada for the reason that I do not believe that very many people in Canada appreciate just the status which is occupied by a naturalized alien in this country. The tremendous immigration of the last 16 years, the influx of Americans to the west and the number of men who have come from all parts of the globe has been so great that here and there you see that the attention of people who think about these matters has been directed to the situation and the demand for a remedy. I have noticed, as many other members have, the communication which has been placed upon our desks, entitled:	' The
Man Without a Country,' in which a magazine article written by Mr. Roden Kings-mill in the ' Busy Man's Magazine ' portrays the ridiculous position in which the naturalized Canadian citizen stands to-day. For instance, the Berlin ' News-Record ', quoting from Mr. Kingsmill, tells us the difference between the passports that are given to naturalized aliens in Canada who

go abroad and to those who are British subjects by birth. I do not know whether the passport is in the language stated by this newspaper, but I have no reason to doubt its accuracy. The statement is that:
When a naturalized citizen applies for a passport his papers read as follows:-
This certificate is granted with the qualification that the said John Smith is only entitled, beyond the limits of the Dominion of Canada, as a matter of courtesy, to the general good offices and assistance of His Majesty's representatives abroad.
This, of course, is no protection at all, and does not enable any one who has come under the advantages of citizenship in this country if he gets in difficulties in travelling anywhere to obtain relief from the representatives of the empire in the slightest degree. I may say that this article in the ' Busy Man's Magazine,' on which this newspaper review is based, tells of a ease in which application was made for some relief in Paris, and where the greatest difficulty was experienced in obtaining recognition on account of the fact that the person applying was only a naturalized British citizen under our Canadian laws. On the other hand the passport issued to a native-born citizen is as follows:
It is requested in the name of His Britannic Majesty, of all those whom it may concern to allow John Smith, a British subject travelling in foreign parts, to (pass freely, and to afford every assistance and protection of which he may stand in need.
The situation that exists in this matter is one that demands a remedy. I am sure that if all the hon. gentlemen in the House fully realized the anomalous position of our law in regard to this matter they would be anxious that the most prompt action should be taken in regard to it and that the anomaly should be removed. I would commend to hon. gentlemen who have not read this little statement entitled, ' The Man without a country,' the facts that are contained in it because in a very illuminative way the situation that exists in regard to citizens coming into this country and obtaining the benefit of naturalization under our laws, is set forth.
To-day the man who comes to Canada and resides for three years goes before a justice of the peace, makes an affidavit to this effect and takes the oath of allegiance. He gets a certificate ultimately from a judge of a court that he has become a British citizen. No doubt hundreds of men who do become naturalized think they become British citizens, I have seen lots of them who thought so. AH that we do as the result of that naturalization is to give these men the right to vote and to a certain extent they are citizens of Canada. . The statement is made that there are in this
parliament hon. gentlemen who are not British subjects in the imperial sense byreason of the fact that they have only become naturalized in the limited Canadian way. Certainly in the western legislatures there are numbers of men who are in that position. It may be that it is only a difference in name, but I apprehend that this is, not the important consideration. We talk, a great deal in this country, and very rightly too it seems to me, about the desirability of drawing closer the ties that bind the empire together, and it is a case-which demands and receives the sympathy and support of every lover of Canada and of the empire. But, if in this the greatese-Dominion of all, with people who come, from _ other lands occupying all the positions that are open to them here, we-continue a situation under which such men, after a residence here of five or six or even ten years cannot call themselves British subjects, and are not entitled to-the protection of the flag or of the empire abroad, we will have a very great departure from that true and proper imperialism which ought to be the very basis of the tie which would bind the whole empire together. I need not elaborate on that..
Would the hon. member allow them to get all these rights on residence of three years in Canada?

The proposal is not to give them these rights on account of three years', but five years' residence in Canada, and after taking the oath of allegiance. That has been the difficulty in the past-that men could go to England, and, after five years' residence, could be naturalized and become citizens of the empire, but if they came to Canada, no matter how long they might live here, could never become citizens of the empire. It is to remove that anomaly that this legislation is proposed. My idea was to impress upon the government the importance and necessity of dealing with the question at an early date to submit to the home authorities as speedily as possible their views with regard to the Bill, so, that if possible we might have legislation from the Imperial parliament before its session is brought to a close. I have no doubt that every other self-governing colony is moving in the matter, and the communications will be made-to the home authorities. I trust the government will deal with it early, so that there may be no delay in the settlement of what seems to me a very important question.

The-question is a very important question as my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) has stated. It has been, agitated now for about twelve years and has not yet been brought to a conclusion sat-

isfactory to us or to any part of the empire. All the time the discussion has been going on, there has been a very strong desire, not only in Great Britain but in the dominions across the seas, for the advantages of imperial citizenship. The very fact that, under these circumstances the matter has been so long under, discussion, without a satisfactory conclusion being reached, indicates the existence of important difficulties in the matter. My hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) says there are important difficulties.
They are (pretty well cleared now.	.

We are very diverse not only in our geographical distribution but in the conditions which underlie nationalities in different parts of the world belonging to the British Empire. But the matter is in a more forward position than it has ever been before. There is a deeper sense of the necessity for some arrangement being come to that shall be adequate to the status of the empire as it at present exists and to the great component parts of the empire outside of the home country. The despatches from which my hon friend has quoted are before the government, and I may tell my hon. friend that a Committee of the Privy Council is now studying die question with a view to sending an answer to the home authorities at the very earliest possible moment.

I should like to say, in reference to the pronouncement by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald)- which I had not expected this evening-that according to my recollection of the discussion that took place in the conference of 1910, the contention of the colonies was in favour a very short time pending the naturalization which would give the party the benefits of the measure now submitted to us by the British government. I think the contention of the dependencies that it was absolutely necessary to make the time short, based upon the fact that persons came to settle definitely in the colonies was well founded. I think that what we have now before us is an evidence of the desire of the British government to meet the great want that' has been discussed during all these years, the necessity for a naturalization which should be recognized throughout the whole British Empire. But it requires to be carefully examined; for I am afraid that people who have been naturalized under the colonial laws will not readily take the additional proceedings which, I understand from my hon. friend's explanation, would be necessary to give the larger rights of citizenship of the empire. A man who has settled in Canada is eager to see Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
the three years expire that he may get his certificate. But once he gets it, it would be very difficult to move him to take the other proceedings necessary to the wider citizenship. He will not do it unless obliged to. That is why, at the conference of 1910, it was so strongly contended that we should all agree upon a fixed time for adoption everywhere, so that one proceeding only should be necessary. Take the case of Canadians who go to the "United States and take out papers there. They very often come back' to Canada; and, though there are. proceedings by which they may resume the quality of British subjects, unless absolutely obliged, they neglect to do so. So, in this new proposal, I think you will find that not readily will the man who has become naturalized take the necessary proceedings to obtain British citizenship throughout the empire. I think that, is worth considering, and also to consider whether, in view of the discussion at that conference, it would not be possible to further urge the British government to recognize a shorter term than five years. In the meantime, we can certainly avail ourselves of this step in the right direction.

With the permission of the House, I will say a word with regard to the points raised by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk). The time stipulated by the colonies varied from nothing at all in New Zealand, up to five years in the mother country. And the New Zealand people were very strong in their desire to obtain that right to give a status as a citizen of the empire to the person coming into their colony, though they required no term of residence, but only some certificate as to character. While there is some force in what the minister (Mr. Monk) says about people taking new proceedings for a second certificate, that does not affect the proposal made here, that you create the machinery under which those who desire to get the rights may obtain them. No machinery exists to-day; and unless you have the machinery provided in some such way as is set forth in this Bill, there is no way by which a newcomer to a colony can acquire status as a citizen of the British Empire.

While it is very desirable from our point of view that we should have, under all circumstances, the fuL privileges of British citizenship, there is a difficulty in putting into a form of words that which will give a right to every person to secure the same privileges, and at the same time preserve- to us within the Dominion of Canada the right to control of our own citizenship within our own borders. In this draft Bill section 8 makes provision, first, that every legislature or government shall have the right to treat
[DOT]2429

different classes of British subjects differently, and that all statutes and ordinances passed by the legislature in regard to citizenship shall have effect of law unless disallowed by His Majesty. These two provisions cover the point that I have in my mind. But I would suggest to the government, in considering this matter, that the points involved in the two parts of that section should be kept very clearly in mind, and considered to be quite as essential as the securing of the full privileges of British citizenship to people who have become naturalized Canadians.

I fully realize the objection pointed out by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk). Perhaps he has forgotten the fact that the naturanzatjon which we are granting at the present time satisfies all the necessities of perhaps ninety-five per cent of the people who come to this country, and become naturalized. It is only in rare instances that a foreigner coming to this country and getting naturalized wishes to leave Canada, and it seems to me that if the provisions found in this draft Bill were carried out we would have machinery by which the one man who wishes to travel abroad can do so under the full rights of a British subject. I had an illustration within the last three months where a gentleman came to me who originally belonged to Armenia. He wanted to get home and he wanted a certificate of -some kind, he called it a passport, and I had to advise him that his naturalization in Canada was of no value whatever excepting as a matter of courtesy. There is a case where, if the law as proposed in the draft Bill were the law of Canada as well as of the empire, that man could have taken advantage of the machinery, and could have qualified himself to receive a certificate. In Canada we have many hundreds of thousands of foreigners coming in and they want to get naturalized as soon as they can under the law and obtain the right of citizenship. Therefore, it seems to me rather a hardship to these people, as well as a disadvantage to the country, if the time is extended to five years instead of three as at present. But if this law were passed they could become citizens of Canada within three years, and if it became necessary, or to their advantage later on, to take advantage of the rest of the machinery, they could do so and thus become citizens of the empire, which really is the obi-ect_ of this legislation. I think if the Minister of Public Work will consider that phase of it he will see that there is not as much difficulty in working it out as he thought at the beginning.

I am pleased indeed that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has brought up this question.
I have taken considerable interest in it for a number of years. As far back as 1900 when representing the Toronto Board of Trade before the Chambers of Commerce of the empire, I presented a resolution asking for the unification of the naturalization laws of the empire. That resolution was endorsed by all the representatives assembled. Theie is no doubt that a great anomaly exists in Canada at the present time with regard to the naturalization of aliens. We are taking away to-day a complete citizenship from all those who come to our country, and we are handing out to them an incomplete citizenship. They lose their naturalization, at least the advantage of their naturalization, the moment they are three miles off our coast, and their naturalization is of no avail in any foreign country except by courtesy of the mother country. What is wanted, in my judgment, is a common system of naturalization for tile whole empire, and whether those conditions exist in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa or Great Britain, they ought to have the same effect throughout ihe British Empire. For instance, a German may come to Canada and be naturalized under our laws, and live here 15 or 20 years, become a member of'this House and have all the rights of citizenship in the empire; but when he goes to Great Britain, to Australia or New Zealand, he is a German, or a Frenchman, or whatever he was when he first came here; he does not belong to the British Empire under the present arrangement. That is a serious anomaly, and it is a great reflection I think upon the empire that this has not been prtt right long years ago. The hon. member for Pictou I think has shown us the necessity of it, and I believe that if this draft Act that he has submitted is adopted throughout the empire, it will be a great advantage to many of our citizens. I quite disagree with the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) when he says that this only affects probably one per cent of our population; I think it will affect at least ten per cent. Many American citizens know that we are taking away from them at the present time complete citizenship in the United States, and are handing them a citizenship that is no good beyond our own Dominion. Only recently I saw a gentleman from Toronto who pointed this out to me. He said he had been in Russia, and he found his passport was little or no good; and he said, to use his own words: This is an outrage upon aliens who are coming to our country. They believe they are really naturalized citizens, and when they go abroad they find that they have no status at all as citizens of the empire. A naturalization law, whatever it may be, should be uniform throughout the empire, and whether the term is three

or five years, once those terms are complied with in any part of the empire, the citizenship that he receives should be just as good in one part of the empire as another. That can only be accomplished by adopting some uniform naturalization law that is good throughout the empire. I think there will be some trouble in some of the words that the member for Pictou drew our attention to, that is, ' an adequate knowledge of English Now we know that ' adequate ' is used quite frequently, and an adequate knowledge of English might mean in the minds of some a very different thing from what it means in the minds of others. There might be difficulty there, but that is a matter of little moment as compared with the difference between a good and real citizenship and a sham citizenship. as we are at present handing out. In the city from which I come we have about 2,000 of a population to whom this is an important and necessary requisite. Many of them are Armenians; we have about 12 or 15 nationalities in the city of Brantford, many of whom want ' to visit their homeland from time to time. Only recently I had two or three cases before me in which I had a great deal of difficulty to get them the necessary passports to travel with safety to their own native shores.
It is well known that some countries of Europe to-day do not acknowledge this passport that we give them and the protection that is afforded to those citizens, and which they believe to be something valid, is of no use when they get there. They are liable to be held by those countries and their wives have been known to have been held there for years after their husbands have become citizens of Canada. They cannot get their families tqgether mi-til they can go over to Europe" and prove to the satisfaction of the country in which their families, are residing that they are now British subjects and entitled to the full rights of British citizenship. I trust that this matter will be pushed, and pushed rapidly, because I foeleive it is one that is becoming an important factor in Canadian national life and it is one of serious consideration for the whole British Empire. Although we boast of the great privilege it is to be a citizen of the British Empire, really all those who are coming to our shores and who have fulfilled the conditions in Canada, find, when they go abroad, on the high seas, or visit any country in Europe, or the United States, or wherever it may be, that their British citizenship is of no avail. I trust that the draft Bill which is presented will be locked into and. if necessary, amended in such a way that the trouble which I have mentioned, will disappear and that a person who becomes a naturalized citizen of Canada will be able to make the proud boast that he is a citi-Mr. COCKSHUTT.
zen of the British Empire, and that he will be able to say that wherever the British flag flies he has a perfect right to citizenship.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to trespass upon the time of the House to any considerable extent, but merely to make a few observations in respect to this matter. I remember that when Mr. Geoffrey Drage and Sir Frederick Pollock visited western Canada some few years ago to interest public opinion on this subject, their efforts were crowned with very considerable success. It seems to me that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), as well as the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, (Mr. Cockshutt), have indicated exactly the difficulties that have been experienced in connection with this matter. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) also dealt with exactly the same sort of difficulty that had to be considered by the Imperial authorities. I think we all agree that it is essential that the autonomous rights of the dependencies of the Empire should be preserved. That is of the utmost importance. Every one of the King's dominions claims the right to pass a statute providing for the naturalization of aliens on such terms as to the legislature of each dependency seems best. That is a sine qua non. They insist upon that right. As the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has just said, the Dominion of New Zealand claims the right to confer citizenship upon a person the next day after he lands and takes the oath of allegiance. Some of the old provinces in Australia exacted live years' residence while we exact only three years, residence.. It is therefore perfectly clear that if there are to be different terms of residence exacted before the domestic tribunals confer rights of citizenship that citizenship should be limited in its application to the boundaries of the country that grants it. Then comes a further question and the difficulty which was experienced is the very difficulty that the hon. member for Edmonton has just referred to, namely, whether or not there might be a uniform arrangement throughout the British Empire as to the terms of citizenship, whether or not a man should have to reside in New Zealand, Australia, Canada or any other British colony or dependency a given number of years absolutely regardless of other considerations and then have conferred upon him, by some domestic tribunal, a citizenship that would be accepted in every portion of the Empire, or whether we should attempt-to deal with it in the way that the draft Bill does, namely, by preserving the right of each colony and of each Dominion to legislate as they please in regard to the requirements which may be exacted from

those who came within her boundaries and who seek the rights of citizenship, and then to adopt one general provision, that in addition to the residence or other qualifications necessary to attain the status of a citizen within the boundaries of the country that conferred the citizenship, the individual should have to live a longer period still in that Dominion before he could obtain Empire citizenship. The Minister of Public Works has pointed out that in the Imperial Conference of 1911 the matter was discussed at length and two schools of thought there found expression. On. the one hand it was strongly urged that there should be a uniform term of residence in the empire and that then the domestic tribunal might confer empire -citizenship. On the other hand there was a suggestion made which is now given force and effect , in the draft Bill before us. It is proposed that while preserving the right that every self-governing colony or dependency may have to make such laws and regulations as to it seems best for granting citizenship to those who come within its boundaries, nevertheless, a residence of five years within that colony or dependency by any person shall entitle him to apply for a certificate of naturalization that- will give him empire citizenship. That is the -purpose of this draft Bill, and I may point out to the hon. m-ember for Edmonton that it preserves to us all our autonomous rights, all our rights to make Such rules and regulations as we may desire in so far as regards the domestic citizenship, while the larger or empire citizenship is to be conferred only when there has been a residence for five years, when the oath of allegiance has been taken to the sovereign and when there has been a certificate given as to the good character of the person in question. With Tegard to the pamphlet that was referred to by the hon. member for Pictou, I happen to know of a case that came under my own observation in which a passport had been issued that did not, make the reservation or provision that is now inserted in a passport issued to naturalized citizens, and it was found in Russia that the person to whom the passport had been issued was wanted for a criminal offence under the laws of that country. He produced hi-s passport, and the passport having been issued upon a form that it should not have been issued upon, international complications arose -by reason of it and it gave a great deal of trouble. They came to the conclusion that a man has no right to have a full passport based only on domestic citizenship and that if he desires to have a pas-sport which will give him the protection of his Britannic Majesty throughout the empire he must have empire citizenship. I entirely approve
of this Bill and I trust that the government, in the words of the despatch to Earl Grey, will give it its earliest possible attention.	_
With regard to early action being taken, South Africa has acted and I am informed that Australia has also acted. Am I correct in that?
There is no advice since November.

I am informed that Australia has acted, or, if it has not acted, has come to a conclusion with regard to it. I trust that Canada will also take immediate action because this is one of the first steps towards a practical realization of the desire that most of us have for some consolidation of imperial interests, for the unity of the empire and the finding of -our proper position in it, so that we may, as the hon. gentleman has just said, be citizens in fact of the Britsh Empire and not of any particular section of it. I welcome legislation along that line and if it will bring about that much desired purpose I trust that the government will early arrive at a conclusion and that they may be able to accept this measure because we realize how difficult it would be to induce New Zealand to change its present domestic law of one -day of residence for the man who takes the oath of allegiance, how difficult it might be to induce the people of Canada to change the standard from 'three years, and I think we should be content to accept this secondary test that has been imposed, namely, residence for five years within the King's dominions and the obtaining of a certificate which gives a man that quality of citizenship that will ensure to him in future empire citizenship. That is a practical kind of imperialism. There are other questions of the same character that might be dealt with in this way in reference to copyrights, patents and the whole series of questions which have been agitating the public mind for -some time. I trust that the government may be able to arrive at an early decision and that they may take advantage of this Bill because it is a Bill that does not work any great hardships and it will provide a remedy for the difficulties that have arisen and will enable persons coming into this country and who have attained to citizenship to be able to say, with ,a little expense and trouble, that they have secured a citizenship that is the highest and best that can be conferred upon any people under any flag under the sun.
But there is -a difficulty in connection with the treaty matter. A German does not lose his citizenship because he becomes naturalized in Canada; a Japanese never loses his citizenship. A Japanese may take the oath of allegiance to our sovereign and I become naturalized, but the moment he

gets back to Japan he is the same Japanese, so far as nationality is concerned, as he, was when he left, Japan. One hon! gentleman who spoke was in error in saying that in England the citizenship was better than here. The Naturalization Act that confers rights on aliens in England is in the same terms as the Act here, our Act being changed only to meet the conditions of our being a Colonial parliament and the other being the Imperial parliament. The Japanese or German who becomes a British subject in England gets no higher right beyond the three mile limit around the British isles than does the man who gets his citizenship here beyond the three mile limit of the Dominion. In both instances what they obtain is subject to treaty rights that exist between the two countries if there be a treaty, and the position he occupies is regulated by the treaty between the land from whence he came and the land to which he comes. On a casual reading of the Bill, I assume that treaty rights are preserved by the saving section which my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) has referred to. I think the House is indebted to the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) for bringing this matter to our attention, and I trust the government will take speedy action because I observe from the deipatohes that the imperial parliament may deal with the question at its coming session, and then legislation will be necessary on the part of the great selfgoverning colonies to manifest their approval of the action taken by the imperial parliament.

I understand that the naturalization of an alien naturalized m Great Britain after having spent five years there, is recognized when he comes to Canada, but the naturalization of an alien naturalized in Canada, does not hold good in Great Britain, where he has to live five years again; the three years he has lived in Canada count for nothing.

My present appreciation of the fact is that we do give^ effect m Canada to the naturalization certificate that comes from any part of the King's dominions. Whether we do that lawfully or not is another matter but I believe that is the practice. I think we will even respect a New Zealand certificate although probably we should not because there a man can take the oath of allegiance and become a citizen the next morning.

A certificate issued in England is recognized throughout the empire, but I do not think we recognize a certificate issued in any of the dependencies, for the same reason that the law has .not force and effect beyond the confines of these dependencies themselves.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply.

I wish to correct a mistake I made last evening in respect to the amount of the 'appropriation for New Brunswick. I stated that for the current year the total amount of the appropriation which was submitted to parliament by the late government, and which was voted, amounted to $506,860.71, but that was only seven-twelfths of the vote, and T should have stated that the total amount for the current year, chargeable to consolidated revenue, is $868,390, whereas the estimate for the coming year chargeable to consolidated revenue for harbours and rivers in the province of New Brunswick, amounts to only $286,925, or less than one-third ot what was provided for in the current year in the estimates submitted by the late government. Then, if you take the total appropriation for New Brunswick in the present estimates, adding the amount charged to capital, including the harbour of St. John, $1,286,925 for the coming year, as against $1,818,390, which the late government submitted for the current year and which was actually voted by parliament. In other words, there is pretty nearly $600,000 less for the harbours and rivers in the province of New Brunswick, so far as these estimates are concerned, than was provided by the late government for the current year. I trust my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) will consider that when he _ comes to make up his supplementary estimates, and that he will open his heart to the province of New Brunswick.

I fear I cannot claim all the credit my hon. friend atributes to me. The $868,000 was comprised in the main and supplementary estimates combined, and as you have not our supplementary estimates yet you cannot establish a comparison.
I am looking forward with hope.
Perhaps when he sees the the supplem-entaries the ihon. gentleman will be inclined to modify liis opinion.

A good deal of discussion has been caused over the fact that a good many items which were voted in the last estimates have been stricken from the *estimates now before the House. If the horn, gentleman intends to replace them in the supplementary estimates., then the procedure is hardly businesslike. I drew attention to New Harbour m any own constituency, for which $10,000 was voted in the estimates of the late government and where the work is absolutely necessary, but that vote is not included in the estimates now before tire House. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) hinted that I might find

it in the supplementary estimates; but why it is left out of the present estimates puzzles me. I might draw attention to the fact that Nova Scotia has been treated even worse than New Brunswick, if we iare to draw a conclusion from the present estimates. In the former estimates Nova Scotia had for harbours and rivers $1,309,166, and in the present estimates only $445,075 is provided'. Therefore, the large sum of $824,066 has disappeared from the estimates of the province of Nova Scotia.
I understand from my hon. friend that a large amount of that money is to be replaced in the supplementary estimates; but why he should go through the form of striking them out of the estimates and putting them back a few weeks later has puzzled me in all this discussion.

It is evident that I have not been able to make my argument clear to my hon. friend. What I stated was that we could not make a comparison between the general appropriation of last year and the appropriation contained in the main estimates for this year, because in the figures which my hon. friend has given for the last year he has included both the main estimates and the supple-mentaries. The main estimates of last year were about $17,000,000, but the supplemen-taries brought that figure up to $25,000,000. Therefore, I stated that to establish a true comparison, my hon. friends would have to wait until they had the whole appropriation of the year; but I did not say that it was intended to restore in the supplementary estimates certain items that were omitted from the main estimates. What I tried to explain was that the government had made its own esti-. mates this year irrespective of what may have appeared in last year's estimates, and if certain items were left out of last year's estimates, that was due to the change of government and the appreciation of what expenditures could be made throughout the country. The same thing was done when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. You would find items in the estimates of one year which disappeared in the following year and after a certain period were restored.
I understand the minister to say that unexpended items voted in. last year's estimates and not appearing in these estimates he intends to drop, and not put them in the supplementary estimates.
Some may appear and some may not.

If a contract has been entered into between the government and a contractor for a public work, are we to
understand that the work will be gone on with even if the item is dropped in the new estimates? On Tuesday last I called the minister's attention to the fact that a contract has been let for a small building, to cost $4,200, at a place called Gravel, although it had appeared in the previous estimates. I want to ask if that work is to be gone on with?
It is my intention to restore that small item, because the work is under contract.

In the estimates for 1912, there were appropriations for various works in the county which I have the honour to represent, amounting to $32,400. In the estimates for 1913, ' I find that this government is generous to the extent of only $500 for the whole county of Antigonish, which has a sea-coast of nearly 100 miles. In these estimates there are.two items-one Arisaig, $1,500 and Livingston's Cove, $2,000, a total of $3,500, of which $3,000 is a revote. In the estimates for 1912, there were the following items: Arisaig, $1,500; Bayfield, $15,000; Cribbin's Point, $1,000; Livingston's Cove, $1,500; McNair's Cove, $5,400; Malignant Cove, $2,300; McAra's Brook, $1,700; and South Lake, $4,000; a total of $32,400. All these have been dropped except the two I have mentioned, wnich appears to be an injustice to the county of Antigonish. The hon. Minister of Public Works assured us a few evenings ago that he was not actuated at all by political considerations in dropping these items. We have to take his assurance, but I cannot understand why these items are not in the estimates for 1913. They aie very important to the people ot these districts, and were recognized by the minister's own engineers as proper to be in the estimates. They were not for works undertaken for election purposes, because nobody expected that there would be an election when there was one. The works must have been regarded by the engineers as necessary. I would ask the minister if it is his intention to make provision for these items in the supplementary estimates, and, if not, on what ground, and on whose recommendation have they been dropped?

I think there must be certain latitude granted hon. members who find themselves in the position of my hon. friend; but when the House gets into committee at this hour, I think the discussion ought to be limited largely to the item before the committee.
I can only repeat to my hon. friend that, the government have not prosecuted those works because they have judged fit to make expenditures elsewhere, which in their opinion are more necessary and more ur-

gent. I cannot explain why works provided for and not begun have not been persisted in by this government. I am here to justify the different items which the government lays before the House, and it must occur to my hon. friend that a long discussion as to the reasons why the government has not brought down other items on other works is not pertinent.

These are not new items, they are only repairs to works already in existence. The minister's argument would be readily understood if it were a ease of new works such as the establishment of a new wharf or breakwater or a new harbour.

speechtext: I beg to remind the hon. member that subsection 5 of Rule 13 says that speeches must be strictly relevant to the time or clause under consideration.

I am not prepared to accept any such interpretation as you, Sir, put on that rule. It would be grossly unfair. No such rule has ever been recognized in this House as that the discussion should be confined to a particular breakwater.

speechtext: I understand that this is a new rule which has not been strictly followed.
When was it made?

Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.) I have to catch a train in a few moments, and as I wish to obtain information with reference to several Prince Edward Island items, I would ask to have one item stand in order that I may ask these questions on another occasion.
We can keep the general item for ' Harbours and Rivers, Prince Edward Island '.

As the minister will remember, on Tuesday last we got into Supply unexpectedly, and passed some items from Saskatchewan and Alberta about which the minister was not then able to give full information as his deputy was not here. A dekgation representing the Board of Trade of Mooseyaw recently visited Ottawa the most notable members being Mr. Willoughby and Dr. Wheeler. They interviewed a number of ministers, and I accompanied them on some of these visits, but I was not able to see the Minister of Public Works with them as I had a previous appointment. Those delegates could properly represent to him the views which they conveyed from Moosejaw with regard to the new building under contract in that city Mr. MONK.
and I understand they made representations to him on a point on which they quite honestly thought they represented the views of that city. I would ask the minister if he _ would advise me as to their representation as to the change of site for that public building, as to what site they wished to have the new public building m Moosejaw moved to. If the minister cannot give the information now I would ask him to obtain it.

I am very sorry, indeed, but my hon. friend must accept my confession that I have not the slightest recollection of what these gentlemen represented. I have been receiving ten or twelve delegations each day for a month past.
The tail end of my remarks constituted a request that the minister would ascertain and advise me.
I did not take anything in writing, I do not remember what they told me at all.	[DOT]

Will the minister ascertain if there is anything official?
Maritime provinces generally-to purchase creosoled timber for works in the maritime provinces generally, $20,000.
Is that to be purchased by tender?
Yes, except where only small quantities are required. Anything of over $5,000 will be bought by tender.
There is a good deal of creosoted timber in the harbour at Inverness. What is the intention of the government in regard to it?
It will be used in repairing the works that we have in that vicinity.

I do not think it can be much used in repairing; the only work there is what was done last year, all the old works having been carried away. There was a vote of over $5,000 for works at Inverness, and I would like to know if the government intends to use this timber for construction by day work or to call for tenders?
There is an item of $5,300 for harbour improvements at Inverness, and if the timber is there it will be used for the purpose of those repairs.

In purchasing this timber, are tenders called for?
If so, to whom is the call for tenders addressed?
I do not think we have purchased much creosoted timber; when a sufficiently large quantity is purchased it is done by tender 'and contract.
How many companies in Canada are in the creosoted timber business?
Not many, but we ask for tenders from those whose names we learn. At one time, this timber was bought from one man only, but there are several now.
Will a copy of the specifications be sent to the representatives of all these concerns?
Any representative who applies for permission to tender, is certainly asked to tender.
Are tenders actually called for through the public press?
Not through the press.
Or do you send out to agents who are in the business of selling creosoted timber?
That is the way it has been done in the past. If this can be improved, I will try to improve it.
Then am I right in assuming that tenders will be invited from all who are in the business?
Yes.

I would ask whether there has been $30,000 already expended, and is this an additional item, or is it a
revote?

It is intended to expend $30,000. The total cost will be about $60,000.
Rivifere-s des Prairies-Improvements of navigation, $25,000.
Is that to carry out the work which was inaugurated on the recommendation of my hon. friend the member for Laval (Mr. Wilson)?

I had already asked that these works be carried out. The hon. member for Laval came in, and in a short time he seemed to be more potent in the House than I was.
Three Rivers harbour-Completion of deep water wharf at west end of harbour, $118,-
000.
(Mr. MONK. I move to add the words ' and for other improvements '.
The hon. .member for Three Rivers is not here. I wished to ask him if it was intended to carry on these works according to the plan which was prepared when I was minister.
Yes. Most of these works are begun, there will be no change.

(Translation.) Before these items for the province of Quebec are all passed, I wish to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works the reason why we do not find in the estimates the amount of $15,000 already voted for the construction of a post office in St. Jacques de l'Achigan, in the county of Montcalm. I have asked for this vote after the property had been purchased, when Mr. Justice Dugas was the member for Montcalm. The site having been purchased, I got this vote for the construction of a post office. When I came in this House in 1909, that amount was put in the estimates, but was not expended because it was too late to begin the works, and as the Department of Public Works did not wish to have the works performed during the winter, I was given the assurance that they would be started in the spring. At the next session I asked once more for that vote of $15,000, which was again granted.

It has been answered to a question asked by myself that the plans had been submitted for examination, and that there had been delays due to some complications in connection with the limits of the property. I would like to know from the minister if it is his intention to have that post office erected this year?	.

I do not know whether there was such an item in last year's estimates or not; if there was, the hon. member should have availed himself of it.	.

(Translation.) I can tell the hon. minister the reason why the item was of no avail after being voted; it is because the estimates were blocked through obstructive discussions by the then members of the opposition.
(Translation.) Why did not you make use of it?

(Translation.) For the present we are net asking the committee

to vote that item. As regards the supplementary estimates, they are being prespared and I cannot now say anything about them.
(Translation.) 1 can assure the hon. minister that this post office is absolutely needed.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the hon. minister how it happens that we do not find this year in the estimates several items concerning my own riding that were in last year's estimates?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Translation.* I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, but I must urge that he should confine himself to the item under consideration. It is a new rule that is rather frequently violated, but I must tell the hon. member that I am compelled to have it observed.
What is the point of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order, as it has been stated before, is that speeches should be strictly relevant to the item under consideration.

(Translation..) Mr. Chairman, I simply want to ask the minister some information relating to the item under consideration. My intention is not to raise any discussion, but I wish to remind him that there were in the estimates for 1912 certain items for works in my county that are omitted this year. I would like to know why they have been omitted and if there will be provision made for those works in the supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Translation.) The item under consideration relates to Three Rivers.

(Translation.) I may tell the hon. member (Mr. Fortier) that our finances did not allow us to put that item in the estimates for next year. We have considered it more prudent and necessary to have some other works performed. As to whether such items will be put in the supplementary estimates, I cannot say this evening as these estimates are still under consideration.

I think we ought not to be too closely bound by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, because it would hamper discussion if we were to adhere to the view which you have presented. I take it that discussion is absolutely relevant to any item in these estimates when a member seeks to compare the utility of a work that is provided for by an item in the estimates with other works of equal, or greater importance, which have been omitted. That is what my hon. friend from Anti-Mr. MONK.
gonish (Mr. Chisholm), was proposing to ao, and what my hon. friend on my night (Mr. Lafortune), was proposing to do. We have the right to say that this committee ought not to be asked to vote an item of $40,000, say, for a work, because, in the same county or province, there are works which are more urgently needed than the item that is asked, and to urge upon the minister that he ought to drop the item that is in the estimates provided he cannot take care of both works and make provision for the other work. Does not my hon. friend remember how, in previous years, he condemned me for putting in items similar to this for wharfs and the improvement of harbours throughout the country? Does not my hon. friend remember the eloquent speeches he made in Committee of Supply urging that the government ought to make provision for starting such works as the Georgian Bay canal, pay more attention to the harbour of Montreal, spend money in nationalizing the harbours, and that it ought not, to use his language, to waste money in the construction of these useless, small wharfs and other works throughout the country? This is the same thing. My hon. friend from Antigonish was seeking to impress upon the committee that works of a more urgent character than those for which he had asked a vote of money had been omitted. It seems to me that this is entirely relevant to the item under discussion. I do not think it should be carried too far or the argument extended too widely, but, it seems to me that it is entirely relevant, and that a member is not discharging his duty unless he calls attention to an injustice to the portion of the province from which he comes.

My hon. friend, I am sure, will appreciate the desire of the Chairman, by his ruling, to keep the discussion down to the item under consideration. I perfectly understand that an hon. member might argue against the adoption of an item, and contend that other works are more urgent and necessary, but my hon. friend, I think, will do me the justice to admit that we have expended several hours on this point as to why the government had omitted from these estimates this year, items which had appeared in last year's estimates for works that were not begun or under contract. That was explained several times, and I think we cannot enter into a full discussion of that point without going beyond the limits which ordinarily should apply under the circumstances.
We have got along very rapidly. We have pa'ssed $600,000 in half an hour.

I was going to suggest to the Minister oi Public Works

that this rule should be leniently enforced even if the Chairman puts the correct interpretation upon it. Of course, the ruling could be avoided by moving an amendment to the motion in each case covering each item. I would like to suggest to the minister that we have allowed him to get along pretty rapidly with his estimates during the session. All the items for harbours and rivers in Quebec have gone through and nearly $1,000,000 have been voted in less than ten minutes. He should allow members from the province of Quebec to discuss any one item in a general way.
Oh, yes.
I take it that when we agree to pass all the items for Quebec it is understood that if any member from Quebec wishes to speak on any item at some other time he will be allowed to do so?
Certainly. Now, we will take up harbours and rivers in Ontario.
Some of the Ontario members who desired to discuss these items are not here.

Suppose my hon. friend goes on with Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia?
Air. AlONK. We have not the information for those provinces, but we have it for Ontario.

We might take Ontario and leave a general item.
Air. AlONK. Yes.
Harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $50,000.

The general item will stand.
Air. AlONK. Yes, stands.
Toronto harbour improvements, $195,000.

Air. AlONK. I visited the work and I found it in excellent condition. There is a very fine breakwater there and the improvements generally seem of the very best quality. There is still very considerable to be done. If we continue that breakwater and the other improvements as they have been going on so far we will be satisfied.

The late government made provision for improvements at Sarnia and entered into an agreement with the Grand Trunk railway with respect to some
necessary property there and it was contemplated to afford facilities urgently required for shipping at that place. The item has been dropped from these estimates and my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) who represents the constituency, feels very strongly about that, and as to the necessity for this work going on. I would like the minister to bring down the papers before these items are concluded, and to be prepared to tell my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) why the item has been dropped, and as to what may be hoped in the near future, as to the prosecution of that work.
Mr. AlONK. I will get the information. I believe there was a tender for that work but it was altogether too high.
